Prabhakar Hegde moved from his native Sirsi in Uttara Kannada to Bengaluru in the nineties to earn a livelihood. He found employment at the iconic Veena Stores in Malleshwaram, and after a few years of working there decided that cooking and serving tiffin was his calling. He went on to open a tiny store in Vidyaranyapura, a far flung locality in North Bengaluru, 23 years ago, a place so remote that back then only a handful of buses would ply there each day. However today, the area has grown into a bustling suburb, and so has Hegde’s Fast Food which is now a cornerstone of the neighbourhood for its idli, vade and a couple of other thindi items. Having received a bunch of recommendations in support of this shop, I visited Hegde impromptu for a chat one evening with him, and also with the locals who have monikered this place as the Veena Stores of Vidyaranyapura.

Please do your best to support tiny small businesses like these that need all the help that they can get for the delicious work they do. Hope you enjoy this one; take care, stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

When Mr Mohan Rao couldn’t find a job in Bengaluru after completing his engineering degree, he hired a cook from Nellore and began a restaurant in 1981. Over time Hotel Navayuga became popular amongst its patrons for the biryanis, kebabs and fries. Its patrons include not just with the common man and hordes of travelers given its location in Gandhinagar, but its fare has also endeared itself to luminaries of Karnataka, most noteworthy being the Dr Rajkumar parivar. 

I was told about this place by Karnataka Ratna, Dr. Puneeth Rajkumar, Appu Sir, and more recently shared a meal with his nephew, Vinay Rajkumar and Anushree when I tasted some of Dr Puneeth Rajkumar’s most favourite dishes here. In this Gourmet On The Road episode, I return to taste some of the delicacies that have transformed Hotel Navayuga from an eatery that was born out of the need for a livelihood to a Bengaluru culinary icon.

I hope you enjoy this very special episode, also catch part one where I visit the kitchens of Navayuga to explore what makes their iconic biryani special, in addition to watching the making of the other favourites here like the chicken kebab, fish fry and more.

Mutton Biryani.summary: A well-rounded, gentle and delicate biryani with aromas and flavors. The  meat is tender and infused with a perfect blend of spices.

Chicken Kebab.summary: Crispy on the outside and moist on the inside, these kebabs offer a delightful crunch with every bite. The chicken is flavorful and juicy, making it a must-try.

Mutton Fry.summary: The mutton fry stands out with tender meat and a rich onion and tomato-based gravy. The blend of spices adds depth and enhances the overall flavor.

Fish Fry.summary: A unique preparation where the fish is both fried and poached, resulting in a crispy exterior and a soft, flavorful interior. The masala coating is infused with coriander and fenugreek, adding aromatic complexity.

Hotel Navayuga, a culinary gem in Bengaluru, has been delighting diners with its authentic Andhra cuisine for over 40 years. Started by Mr. Mohan Rao, the restaurant is a testament to his commitment to preserving traditional flavors and cooking techniques. The biryani here is cooked on a wood-fired stove, imparting a unique smoky flavor. The restaurant's popularity is evident in the constant stream of patrons, from locals to celebrities like the late Dr. Puneeth Rajkumar. The mutton biryani is a must-try, known for its tender meat and well-balanced flavors. Other highlights include the crispy chicken kebab, flavorful fish fry, and the rich mutton fry. The Andhra meals offer a wholesome experience with a variety of dishes and flavors. With its dedication to quality and authentic flavors, Hotel Navayuga continues to be a beloved dining destination in Bengaluru.  

Highlight: The use of a wood-fired stove for cooking biryani, a traditional method that sets Hotel Navayuga apart, adds a distinct smoky flavor to their signature dish.

I was first introduced to Hotel Navayuga during the course of my most memorable meal, with Karnataka Ratna, Dr Puneeth Rajkumar, Appu Sir. We were relishing a traditional jolada rotti oota, but somewhere our conversation veered to tasting a biryani during our next meal. Alas, that wasn’t meant to be, but deep down I feel that if it would have been at Hotel Navayuga, a 40-year-old eatery that Appu Sir spoke about quite fondly. I did make a visit to the eatery later, to record a tribute episode to commemorate his last film over a meal with his nephew, Vinay Rajkumar and Anchor Anushree. It was also during the course of this meal that I decided I must return to film a full-fledged Gourmet On Episode.

I hope you enjoy part one of this episode, where I visit the kitchens of Navayuga to explore what makes their iconic biryani special, in addition to watching the making of their other favourites like the chicken kebab, fish fry and more.

Over the last couple of years, I have received innumerable requests from our viewers to taste the khaali dosae at Chitradurga’s popular Sri Lakshmi Bhavan Tiffin Room. And so, on a recent drive through the area, I stopped at this 68-year old institution where I enjoyed my short conversation with the humble second-generation proprietor, Mr Mahabala, and also caught the making of what is perhaps one of the fluffiest khaali dosae that I’ve eaten. Khaali means ‘empty’ in kannada, there is no oil deployed in the dosae’s cooking, but ironically the tradition here is to serve it with some tuppa (ghee), and palya (potato stuffing) to make for an enjoyable, filling thindi. And they say, you shouldn't leave here without tasting their soft gulab jamun, which is what i savoured too in addition to a lovely idli sambar.

Hope you enjoy this tiffin watch, definitely pencil the place into your travel plans when in and around Chitradurga. Happy eating.

He praises its fluffy texture and the crispy exterior and describes the combination of flavors as both delicious and satisfying. He also tries their Idli Sambar and Gulab Jamun, both of which he highly recommends.  What makes this place unique is their dedication to tradition and the unchanged taste of their dishes, which keep customers coming back for more.

Not enjoying his vocation as a public works contractor, Satyanarayana Reddy converted a part of his home into a rustic eatery in Chitradurga, seeking to serve non vegetarian delicacies made to his wife’s recipes. The eatery had no signboard for many years, but gained immense popularity amongst locals for its unique mutton and chicken dishes. The atmosphere of this 31-year-old eatery is rather rudimentary, but the fare served here is the sort that will have you reminiscing its robust flavours well into your journey.

When work brought Arpita and Sujoy Das to Bengaluru 13 years ago, they yearned for the flavours of Kolkata's street fare, more specifically the Calcutta kathi roll. Since they could find none, Arpita decided to open a tiny 150 square feet shop cooking and serving up this quintessential Kolkata eat-as-you-go treat. It was only a matter of time before Sujoy quit his advertising job to support this small enterprise that has since built for itself a loyal following not only for its rolls that are made completely in house, including the spice mix with a few ingredients shipped from Kolkata, but also their Kolkata style kebabs and biryani in recent times. I visit them for a late lunch and make a meal of three tasty kathi rolls.

After completing his education, Kamalesh Gowda decided to put up a vada pav stall and deploy his father’s recipe of a spicy chutney that the latter had picked up during his days in Mumbai decades ago. Tucked in a quiet bylane of BTM 2nd Stage in South Bengaluru, one-man army, Kamlesh goes about his business quietly, particular about his ingredients resulting in his regular customers being quite vocal for him. Which is how I discovered him through a twitter poll a few weeks ago. Please do support small enterprises like Modern Vada Pav Centre that are trying to earn an honest living serving delicious fare.

When Mrs. Padma and her husband, Prakash mulled the idea of a new street food enterprise in the throes of the pandemic to stay afloat, they thought it would be unique to introduce the pizza but in a flavourful avatar that would resonate the punchy flavours that people expect in street fare. And thus was born Amma’s Italian Pizza, first on a cart and now a van. Padma Amma experimented with vegetarian topping combinations for days on end at her home, also sharpening her secret recipe for a piquant pizza sauce, a sprightly medley of herbs, spices, sour, sweet and heat. From a spiced-up Margherita to a Karnataka pizza that basically incorporates almost every ingredient she has available, Amma’s pizzas are slowly but surely gaining favour with the locals of Koramangala, South Bengaluru for her hygienic approach to using fresh quality ingredients and creating flavours of the sort that appeal to most mainstream palates. The name may say ‘Italian’, but these are the sort of pizzas that resonate the ‘kadak’, street vibes of namma ooru, Bengaluru.

In our last Old Delhi outing this season, we stumbled upon the best biryani that we tasted in the walled city. Getting to Taufiq Dilpasand Biryani Point requires some effort given its location in the inner recesses of Galli Haveli Azam Khan, a bit of a walk from Jama Masjid. The shop itself is a little more than a window, but the biryani that emerges from the copper pots here has endeared itself to biryani lovers in the know for a quarter of a century now. Hope you enjoy this one too.

They call Haji Mohd Hussain’s fried chicken the KFC of Old Delhi, a moniker well earned by the hard working septuagenarian for his single minded focus to making his version of a double fried, crisp and juicy, spicy chicken. Speaking of one-dish eateries, further down the road, one also finds Shabrati Nahari Shop that has been making a slow-braised eight-hour nahari twice a day each day since 1954. And in between the fried chicken and nahari, I also gulped down a few glasses of mohabbat ka sharbat, a delightful refreshing concoction that I instantly fell in love with.

Park aside whatever notions you may have of the butter chicken, for Purani Dilli’s most famous Aslam Butter Chicken is anything but that. Made to a seemingly simple recipe with secret masalas, this roasted and charcoal grilled chicken bathed in copious amounts of molten butter has built for this Jama Masjid eatery an iconic status over a span of 25 years. We catch the making of this indulgent chicken tikka, but before that take respite in the reinvigorating offerings of a tea stall that goes back seven or eight decades.

What began as Mrs. Geetha Shivakumar’s home cooking initiative 23 years ago to bridge with farmers and bring a seasonal produce to Bengaluru’s consumers in a myriad range of savoury and sweet delicacies is now a culinary institution called the Avarebele Mela. Farmers congregate from Magadi, Karnataka bringing the pick of their crops and the cooks from Shree Vasavi Condiments cook up a host of preparations, each one featuring the avarebele. I was recently invited to open this festival with a host of other dignitaries including Mrs. Sudha Murthy, Sihi Kahi Chandru Sir and others. Hope you enjoy this vlog account of my experience there. The mela runs through 9th January 2023 at National College Grounds, Basavanagudi, Bengaluru.

Take care; stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

Bengaluru’s Annual Avarebele Mela at Sri Vasavi Vaisistha THindi, VV Puram Food Street, Farm to Food, Hyacinth Beans, Hithkabele Masala Vade, Hithkabele Bonda, Avarebele Dose - Hithkabele Saru, Hithkabele Akki Rotti, Avarebele Mosaru Kodubale, Hithkabele Holige, Hithkabele Honey Jalebi, Payasa, Ellavare, Street Food

Now in its 20th year, Bengaluru’s annual Avarebele Mela that celebrates the Bengaluru bean in an array of ‘snacky’ preparations, goes back to a time when farmers from in and around Bengaluru would congregate in VV Puram to sell their harvest of Avarekai. Given the bean’s short shelf life, any unsold produce would be thrown away. Which prompted Mrs Geetha Shivakumar, owner of Sri Vasavi Vasisitha Mane Thindi to put together a food festival that would make use of the Avarebele. And thus began a unique collaboration between farmers and a food entrepreneur that now has Bangalore’s food lovers congregating here for their share of deliciousness.

Food Lovers’ Editor visits the mela and tasted a delicious smorgasbord of preparations, from vade to bonda to dose to hollige to rotti to jalebi to payasa to pootharekulu, with one ingredient in common, the avarebele. Enjoy!

Hithkabele Masala Vade
A top draw at the mela, and also all year around, one can taste the freshness of coriander and dill in this spicy hithabele masala vade. 
Rs. 20 (usd 0.3) for 2 nos.
9/10

Hithkabele Bonda
A tad mellow in flavour, the bonda benefits from the weight of the avarekalu. It’s a pleasing snack, but fails to make as impactful an impression on the palate as the masala vade. 
Rs. 20 (usd  0.3) for 2 nos.
7/10

Avarebele Dose - Hithkabele Saru
The most popular item at the mela, this dosa is topped with a spirited mix of avarebele, coriander, dil and onions. 
Rs. 60 (usd 0.8)
9.5/10

Hithkabele Akki Rotti
The akki roti is toasted nice and thin, and crispened around the edges making for a delightful crunch. 
Rs. 50 (usd 0.7)
8.5/10

Avarebele Mosaru Kodubale
Crisp and crunchy on the bite, but chewy as you linger on this bangle-shaped jeera and ajwain flavoured treat made of steamed rice flour, yoghurt and avarebele.
Rs. 30 (usd 0.4) for 4 nos.
8/10

Hithkabele Holige
Dripping with ghee and stuffed with tuvar dal, jaggery and hithkabele, one can taste the lingering aroma of cardamom on the palate. 
Rs. 30 (usd 0.4)
8.5/10

Hithkabele Honey Jalebi
The jalebi are a light pista green in colour from the avarebele which lends its strength to the fermented batter and renders the jalebis cripier and also lends it a tart edge.  
Rs. 20 (usd 0.3) for 4 nos.
8.5/10

Payasa
The avarebele payasa is smokey in its flavour. Although made with gas gase, poppy seeds, one does not taste the nuttiness of the ingredient. 
Rs. 30 (usd 0.3)
6.5/10

Ellavare
Sesame seeds, coconut milk, avarebele and jaggery come together in this thick dessert. I quite enjoyed the crunch of the fresh coconut and the earthy sweetness of the jaggery.
Rs. 30 (usd 0.3)
7/10

Putharekulu
The avarebele makes its way into the putharekulu as well. However, I’m tasting more of the wrap in this version as compared to the filling and that takes away from the enjoyment of what is otherwise an interesting sweet.
Rs. 30 (usd 0.3)
6/10

The highlight of the experience is undoubtedly the Chicken Changezi, a unique and flavorful dish that lives up to its reputation. The Mutton Seekh Kebab also receives high praise for its delicious taste and tender texture. While the Mutton Biryani is considered decent, the star of the show remains the Chicken Changezi, a must-try for anyone visiting the restaurant.  The video also features a visit to Haji Nizamuddin Shahi Sheermal, where we get to savor the rich and crispy Shahi Sheermal, a delightful treat for the taste buds.  What sets this food tour apart is the emphasis on experiencing the true essence of Old Delhi's culinary offerings.

https://goo.gl/maps/QN7cVusJLjjrVf7s5.summary: This episode of Old Delhi Food Tour takes us to Al Jawahar, a popular eatery near Jama Masjid, where we savor their signature Chicken Changezi, a flavorful roasted chicken in gravy. The dish lives up to its hype, with tender chicken and a well-balanced tomato-onion based gravy.  We also try their Mutton Seekh Kebab and Mutton Biryani.  The kebabs are a delight, flavorful and less fatty compared to others, while the biryani boasts tender mutton cooked to perfection.  The rice in the biryani is decent, but the highlight is definitely the meat.  To top it off, we head to Haji Nizamuddin for their unique Shahi Sheermal, a rich, fortified bread cooked in a tandoor. Overall, Al Jawahar proves to be a great spot to enjoy some classic Mughlai dishes in the heart of Old Delhi

Mango Kulfi.summary: A whole mango is cooked, stuffed with kulfi, and then sealed back. It's a unique and flavorful dessert that combines the sweetness of mango with the richness of kulfi.

Pomegranate Kulfi.summary: Similar to the mango kulfi, this dessert features a whole pomegranate filled with kulfi. The tartness of the pomegranate complements the sweetness of the kulfi, creating a refreshing treat.

Phalsa Kulfi.summary: This kulfi is made with phalsa, a tart and tangy fruit. It has a more icy texture than the mango and pomegranate kulfis and is a great palate cleanser.

Jamun Kulfi.summary: Made with ripe jamun fruit, this kulfi has a deep purple color and a slightly tart, tangy flavor. It's a refreshing and flavorful dessert that's perfect for a hot day.

Established in 1956, Giani’s Di Hatti is a legendary Old Delhi institution for its chole bhature, chana chawal, rabri falooda, malai lassi, among other offerings. Tended to by the third generation of a family that migrated to Delhi post partition, the old fashioned fare here is the sort that endears to locals for its wholesome goodness laced with a tinge of nostalgia. When in Chandni Chowk, Giani’s Di Hatti is a definite must-visit.

In this sweet and savoury episode, we cover three must-visit Old Delhi favourites. Our first stop is at Hazari lal Jain Khurchan Wale where we taste the pure dairy goodness of a traditional reduced milk dessert and some more. This is followed by a piquant introduction to Old Delhi’s famous Lotan Chole Kulche. This is perhaps the spiciest chole that I have tasted, and the reason, I am told, for its popularity especially in Delhi’s nippy winters. Our last halt, Padam Chaat comes as a wonderful respite for its tantalizing chaats that work marvelously well to tease our taste buds with a broad array of textures and delicate flavours.

Authentic Maharashtrian Food at Suryawanshi Restaurant, Bengaluru, Bangalore, Kolhapuri Mutton, Mutton Thali, Pune Vegetarian Food, Pandra Rasa, Tamba Rasa, Misal pav, Vada Pav, Sabudana Vada, Whitefield, Bangalore, Prawn Fry, Pomfret Fry, Malvan Fish Curry, eating out in bengaluru, bangalore,  food trail, must try restaurant 

When Kailash Suryawanshi moved from Kolhapur to Bengaluru with his family nearly a decade ago, the one cuisine he couldn’t get any of was his own. Such was his yearning for food from his land, that this entrepreneur decided to take upon himself the onerous task of introducing Bengaluru to authentic Marathi fare. After months of travel through the hinterlands of Maharashtra, gleaning recipes and cooks, Suryawanshi was born, a restaurant where conversations in Marathi waft through the dining room, as if in endorsement of the food served here.

In this throwback #gourmetontheroad episode, I catch up with the Suryawanshi family and also tuck into some delicious Maharashtrian cuisine, tasting everything from Pandra Aani Tambda Rasa, Misal Pav, Sabudana Vada, Puneri Veg Thali, Kolhaprui Mutton Thali, Puran Poli, Amras, Shrikhand and more. Enjoy!

This humble eatery, established over 40 years ago, offers a delightful culinary experience with their special vegetarian thali. Priced at an incredibly affordable ₹130, this unlimited thali features a diverse selection of dishes, each prepared with care and bursting with flavors. From the simple yet satisfying tomato soup to the crispy cabbage poriyal, the comforting vegetable korma, and the flavorful sambar and rasam, every item on the thali reflects the essence of home-style Tamil cooking. The star of the show is undoubtedly the Kashi halwa, a rich and decadent dessert that perfectly concludes the meal. What sets Sri Sai Vihar apart is its commitment to serving delicious food at honest prices, making it a favorite among locals and a must-try for visitors exploring Salem's culinary scene.

A restaurant that has been in existence since 1958, Mangala Vilas in Salem is known for its entirely non-vegetarian menu that features homestyle dishes made using spice blends ground fresh every day. 

In this throwback episode, we visit their relatively newer, 15-year-old outlet of Mangala Vilas on New Bus Stand Road Salem to savour a hardcore robustly flavoured non-vegetarian feast! 

Before getting to the table, we step inside the kitchen to watch the making of the signature Mangala masala that is used in the making of every dish on the restaurant’s menu. And taste 12 of the most popular dishes here  - Kothu Parotta, Vanjaram Fry, Naatu Kozhi Leg Roast, Mutton Pepper Fry and more!

best_dishes.name: Vanjaram Fry
best_dishes.summary: Perfectly cooked fish with a crispy masala crust. The masala isn't spicy and complements the fish well. A squeeze of lemon enhances the flavors.

best_dishes.name: Mutton Curry
best_dishes.summary: Tender mutton pieces in a creamy curry. The mutton is cooked for over an hour, making it incredibly soft and flavorful. The fat melts in your mouth, adding to the richness.

best_dishes.name: Naatu Kozhi Roast
best_dishes.summary: A large leg piece of country chicken cooked with a spicy and flavorful masala. The chicken is tender and pink, having absorbed all the spices.

best_dishes.name: Chicken Pepper Fry
best_dishes.summary: Crispy and dry chicken cooked with pepper and curry leaves. The flavors are intense and the chicken is cooked to perfection.

best_dishes.name: Mutton Pepper Fry
best_dishes.summary: Similar to the chicken pepper fry, but with mutton. The mutton flavor is more prominent than the pepper in this dish.

best_dishes.name: Naatu Kozhi Liver
best_dishes.summary: Country chicken liver cooked to a powdery softness. The flavors are deep and savory.

best_dishes.name: Mutton Chukka
best_dishes.summary: Mutton cooked with gravy that has been reduced slightly, resulting in a semi-gravy consistency. The mutton is cooked perfectly, as always.

best_dishes.name: Kothu Parotta
best_dishes.summary: Parotta mashed up with eggs, onions, tomatoes, curry leaves, pepper, and other spices. A comforting and flavorful dish.

This video is a throwback to a visit to Mangala Vilas in Salem, a restaurant known for its traditional non-vegetarian Tamil cuisine, particularly Kongunadu dishes. The restaurant has been serving delicious food since 1958.  

The host takes us behind the scenes to see the preparation of their signature Mangala masala, a blend of 15 spices that forms the base of their dishes. They use fresh, high-quality ingredients, including country chicken and mutton. 

The dishes are praised for their robust flavors and the perfect cooking of the meat.  The host tries various dishes, including Vanjaram Fry, Mutton Curry, Naatu Kozhi Roast, and Pepper Fry. Each dish is unique and highlights the restaurant's expertise in South Indian non-vegetarian cuisine. 

Highlight: What makes Mangala Vilas stand out is its dedication to traditional cooking methods and the use of fresh, local ingredients. The host emphasizes the tenderness and juiciness of the meat, a testament to their slow cooking process and the use of the special Mangala masala. The popularity of the restaurant among locals further reinforces its authenticity and delicious food.

shiv sagar, mumbai pav bhaji, bengaluru, pav bhaji making, vegetarian restaurant, eating out in bangalore, bengaluru food trail, vegetarian, popular restaurant

A dish that finds its origins in leftover vegetables tossed by street vendors into an inexpensive but tasty mash and served with local bakery bread as cheap sustenance to Bombay’s mill workers at the turn of the last century, the pav bhaji evolved to its buttery, cheesy, somewhat indulgent avatar courtesy savvy restaurateurs in the seventies and eighties. My memories of a Mumbai pav bhaji go back to Shiv Sagar, Juhu and Vile Parle, a hop and a skip away from college, where I relished many a plate. So when a craving for the Mumbai style pav bhaji hit me one cold evening, I found my way to the Bengaluru outpost of Shiv Sagar, where brothers Ram and Shyam, second generation restaurateurs trained in the Mumbai restaurant, dish up this quintessential Mumbai fast food that is quite close to the real deal. 

Hope you enjoy this throwback episode. Take care, stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

The dish, originating from Mumbai, was traditionally made with leftover vegetables for mill workers but evolved into a buttery, flavorful street food.  The restaurant sources its spices from Surat, using a secret blend for their Pav Bhaji. Key ingredients include a special red chili paste, various vegetables, and a generous amount of butter. Kripal finds the taste nostalgic, reminiscent of Mumbai's Pav Bhaji, despite the difference in water quality affecting the taste slightly. He ends the meal with a Kesari Falooda, a sweet and refreshing dessert.

If you love your seafood, Ambhika Hotel in Kozhikode is where you have to be for their legendary seafood sadhya that serves up over 18 varieties on a banana leaf. From pickles to chutneys to porichatu, peera, avial, pulisherry, aviyal, curries, kappa to even the sambar and rasam, every sadhya staple is made in a seafood version! Kingfish, prawns, crabs, squid, sardines, pomfret, mussels, silverfish… there’s every conceivable marine form on offer on the banana leaf.

samudra sadhya.summary: A seafood feast with 19 varieties of seafood prepared in Kerala style. It includes pickles, chutneys, fries, curries, and more, all made with fresh seafood like kingfish, prawns, crabs, squid, sardines, and mussels.

Avoli Fry (White Pomfret).summary: White Pomfret fish fried and then wrapped in a flavorful masala, cooked in a banana leaf. It offers a unique taste with a blend of spices and the freshness of the fish.

Murumin Fry.summary: A crispy fried fish dish where the Murumin fish is first fried and then coated with a special spicy masala. The masala adds a distinct flavor to the fish, making it a must-try.

https://maps.app.goo.gl/jNrXtA7UcDELR4fm.summary: This video takes you on a culinary journey to Hotel Ambika in Kozhikode, Kerala, to experience their legendary seafood sadhya, Samudra Sadhya. The highlight of the video is the sheer variety of seafood served on a banana leaf, with 19 unique dishes. From pickles to chutneys, fries, curries, and more, each dish is a testament to Kerala's love for seafood. The host savors popular dishes like the spicy Kingfish pickle, flavorful seafood avial, delicious mussels roast, and the unique Kappa made with fish. The highlight, however, is the Samudra Sadhya, a seafood platter that goes beyond the ordinary, showcasing the chef's creativity and expertise in seafood preparations. The host highly recommends visiting Hotel Ambika if you are in Kerala and craving an unforgettable seafood experience.

Mushroom Dumpling.name: Mushroom Dumpling
Mushroom Dumpling.summary: This purple-looking dumpling is filled with a mix of mushrooms, including oyster, button, and shiitake, all brought together with an Asian white sauce and a touch of truffle oil. Topped with bell peppers for a delightful crunch.

Spinach Dumpling.name: Spinach Dumpling
Spinach Dumpling.summary: This vibrant green dumpling features a filling of corn and carrots, encased in a spinach-flavored skin. The strained spinach puree not only adds a beautiful color but also a subtly sweet and earthy flavor.

Pumpkin Dumpling.name: Pumpkin Dumpling
Pumpkin Dumpling.summary: This delightful dumpling features a translucent skin, allowing you to peek at the flavorful roasted pumpkin and water chestnut filling. A sprinkle of parsley on top adds a touch of freshness.

Carrot Dumpling.name: Carrot Dumpling
Carrot Dumpling.summary: This bright orange dumpling is filled with a crunchy and savory mixture of broccoli, celery, chili, and garlic. The carrot flavor shines through, complementing the other vegetables beautifully.

Wasabi and Edamame Dumpling.name: Wasabi and Edamame Dumpling
Wasabi and Edamame Dumpling.summary: This unique dumpling combines the delicate flavor of edamame with a subtle hint of wasabi. The yellow hue comes from a mix of custard powder and pumpkin puree, creating a visually appealing and delicious treat.

Chinese Cabbage and Bok Choy Dumpling.name: Chinese Cabbage and Bok Choy Dumpling
Chinese Cabbage and Bok Choy Dumpling.summary: This delicate dumpling features a translucent skin that reveals the flavorful filling of Chinese cabbage and bok choy. A touch of pomegranate on top adds a burst of fruity sweetness.

Prawn Hargau.name: Prawn Hargao
Prawn Hargau.summary: This classic dim sum dish features succulent prawns encased in a delicate, translucent wrapper. The prawn filling is perfectly seasoned, offering a delightful balance of savory and slightly sweet flavors.

Squid Ink Seafood Dumpling.name: Squid Ink Seafood Dumpling
Squid Ink Seafood Dumpling.summary: This visually striking dumpling gets its black color from squid ink, which also adds a subtle savory flavor. The filling is a delicious combination of shrimp, fish, and squid, topped with a dollop of egg white and a sprinkle of Tobiko (flying fish roe).

Aromatic Chicken Dumpling.name: Aromatic Chicken Dumpling
Aromatic Chicken Dumpling.summary: This popular dumpling is packed with flavor, thanks to a blend of aromatic spices like kaffir lime and lemongrass. The chicken filling is juicy and tender, with a hint of heat from fresh red chilies.

Duck Dumpling with Fresh Plums.name: Duck Dumpling with Fresh Plums
Duck Dumpling with Fresh Plums.summary: This unique dumpling pairs tender duck meat with the sweet and slightly tart flavor of fresh plums. The combination is surprisingly harmonious, creating a rich and flavorful experience.

Basil Chicken Dumpling.name: Basil Chicken Dumpling
Basil Chicken Dumpling.summary: This fragrant dumpling features tender chicken infused with the refreshing flavor of basil. The dumpling is topped with a sprinkle of garlic, which adds a subtle pungency and enhances the overall savory profile.

Char Siu Chicken Dumpling.name: Char Siu Chicken Dumpling
Char Siu Chicken Dumpling.summary: This flavorful dumpling features a rich and savory filling of char siu chicken, coated in a sweet and smoky Chinese barbecue sauce. The sauce is infused with ginger and garlic, adding layers of flavor to every bite.

Fish Dumpling.name: Fish Dumpling
Fish Dumpling.summary: This delicate dumpling features a flavorful filling of fresh water fish, seasoned with black pepper and enhanced by the crunchy texture of spring onions. A sprinkle of toasted sesame seeds adds a nutty aroma and a hint of bitterness.

Skinless Prawn and Spinach Dumpling.name: Skinless Prawn and Spinach Dumpling
Skinless Prawn and Spinach Dumpling.summary: This innovative dumpling features succulent prawns wrapped in blanched spinach, steamed to perfection and served in a beautiful banana flower. The absence of a traditional wrapper allows the flavors of the prawn and spinach to shine through, complemented by a drizzle of savory bean sauce.

https://goo.gl/maps/domXSFV6esnRKh54A.summary: This video takes us on a culinary journey to Sriracha, a renowned Pan-Asian restaurant in Bengaluru, India. Hosted by food enthusiast Kripal Amanna of Gourmet on the Road, the episode celebrates the vibrant Festival of Colors, Holi, by showcasing a colorful array of 14 unique and flavorful dim sums. The video begins with a trip to the kitchen, where we witness the meticulous craftsmanship of the dim sum chefs. We see how each dumpling is carefully folded and crimped, ensuring a perfect balance of texture and flavor.  From classic vegetarian options like the Mushroom Dumpling with its earthy aroma of truffle oil and the refreshing Spinach Dumpling to more adventurous choices like the Duck Dumpling with Fresh Plums and the Squid Ink Seafood Dumpling, there’s something to satisfy every palate. Throughout the tasting, Kripal highlights the unique characteristics of each dim sum, from the translucent skin of the Prawn Hargau to the bold flavors of the Char Siu Chicken Dumpling. He emphasizes the importance of eating dim sums hot to fully appreciate their delicate flavors and textures. The video concludes with a call to action, encouraging viewers to visit Sriracha and experience the delightful world of dim sums for themselves.

Kodu Bale.summary: Crispy and stretchy savory snack made from buttermilk and rice flour, shaped like bangles.

Butterfruit Juice.summary: Refreshing juice made from fresh avocados sourced from the Nilgiris.

Dry Fruit Milkshake.summary: A healthy and filling milkshake with a blend of dry fruits and milk.

Masala Soda.summary: A refreshing and spicy soda, a popular drink on the streets of Bangalore.

47 years ago, Janab Ahmed Basha Sahib set up a modest eatery in Vaniyambadi, a town in Tirupattur district of Tamil Nadu, famous for its leather industry. The fare at Ahmedia Hotel was mostly Mughlai,  inspired by the culinary traditions of erstwhile North Arcot principality. Over decades the kitchens here have perfected time-honored recipes, amongst them a wood-fire-cooked biryani that, unusual for Tamil Nadu, favours the basmati over seeraga samba rice. I discovered Ahmedia three years ago on a #gourmetontheroad tour through the region when I met the founder and his enterprising sons. Janab Ahmed Basha has passed on since, but his sons seem determined to build on their father’s legacy. And have now opened a massive 25,000 sq. ft., 250-seat Ahmedia branch on the Bengaluru Chennai highway with the conveniences required to cater to travellers. I visited them on a recent trip to Chennai, where I tasted most of my favourite dishes here, including the biryani that has put Vaniyambadi on the culinary map.

Mutton Nalli Soup.name: Mutton Nalli Soup
Mutton Nalli Soup.summary: A light broth delicately flavored with green chili, coriander, and spices, slow-cooked with bone marrow for a flavorful and comforting experience.

Brain Pepper Fry.name: Brain Pepper Fry
Brain Pepper Fry.summary: Soft and creamy brain cooked with a generous amount of pepper and curry leaves. The balance of flavors highlights the rich, buttery taste of the brain without being overpowering

Mutton Chukka.name: Mutton Chukka
Mutton Chukka.summary: Tender pieces of mutton cooked dry on the outside but juicy on the inside, seasoned with a flavorful blend of spices.

Mutton Liver Fry.name: Mutton Liver Fry
Mutton Liver Fry.summary: A flavourful liver fry with a perfect balance of spices, this dish is a must-try for those who enjoy the bold taste of liver.

Mutton Kidney.name: Mutton Kidney
Mutton Kidney.summary: Well-cleaned kidney cooked to perfection with a blend of green spices. The kidney is tender and lacks any unpleasant ammonia flavor.

Mutton Attukal (Paya) Fry.name: Mutton Attukal (Paya) Fry
Mutton Attukal (Paya) Fry.summary: A crispy and flavorful pepper fry, the gelatin in the paya provides a crunchy texture, making it an interesting and delicious dish.

Mutton Biryani.name: Mutton Biryani
Mutton Biryani.summary: Aromatic and flavorful biryani made with long-grain basmati rice. The rice is infused with the flavors of the meat and spices, and the mutton is tender and falls off the bone.

Chicken Biryani.name: Chicken Biryani
Chicken Biryani.summary: Flavorful biryani made with tender chicken and fragrant basmati rice. Though not as rich as the mutton biryani, the chicken biryani is still a satisfying and enjoyable dish.

https://goo.gl/maps/eqCLGkb9Fz99wVJH6.summary: Ahmedia Restaurant, a culinary landmark on the Bengaluru-Chennai highway, continues a legacy dating back to 1975. This spacious and modern establishment boasts a wide array of traditional Mughlai and Tamil Nadu dishes, including their renowned wood-fire cooked biryani.  What sets Ahmedia apart is its commitment to time-honored recipes and the use of high-quality ingredients. The mutton dishes are a testament to their expertise, with highlights including the melt-in-your-mouth Mutton Nalli Soup, the flavorful Brain Pepper Fry, and the tender Mutton Chukka. The star of the show, however, is undoubtedly the Mutton Biryani. Made with long-grain basmati rice, the biryani is infused with the rich flavors of the meat and spices, creating a culinary masterpiece that has earned its place on the map. While the mutton reigns supreme, the Chicken Biryani also holds its own, offering a satisfying and flavorful experience for chicken enthusiasts. Ahmedia Restaurant is not just a stop on the highway but a destination for food lovers seeking an authentic taste of tradition and culinary excellence.

Dal Poori.name: Dal Poori
Dal Poori.summary: A hearty and flavorful puri made with moong dal, served with a mellow and slightly tangy aloo badi sabzi. The puri has a satisfying weight and a bit of bite to its texture.

Methi Poori.name: Methi Poori
Methi Poori.summary: A fragrant and flavorful puri infused with the aroma of kasuri methi (dried fenugreek leaves). It pairs well with the subtle flavors of the aloo badi sabzi. The fenugreek adds a unique taste to the puri

Aloo Wadi Ki Subzi.name: Aloo Wadi Ki Subzi
Aloo Wadi Ki Subzi.summary: A delicately spiced gravy-based dish with potatoes and lentil dumplings (wadi). The flavors are subtle, with hints of amchur (dry mango powder) and hing (asafoetida), providing a well-balanced taste.

Chana.name: Chana
Chana.summary: A simple yet satisfying chickpea curry. The chickpeas are cooked to perfection and coated in a flavorful gravy with a mild spiciness.  It is recommended to pair it with the Methi Puri for a burst of flavor.

Samosa.name: Samosa
Samosa.summary: A crispy and flaky samosa with a flavorful potato filling.  The samosa is well-seasoned with a good balance of spices, including cumin, coriander, and amchur.

Kachori.name: Kachori
Kachori.summary: A deep-fried, crispy pastry filled with a generous amount of spiced lentil stuffing. The kachori at Panditji Ras Bana Rahe stands out for its coarse lentil texture, adding a unique and satisfying element to the dish.

Jalebi.name: Jalebi
Jalebi.summary: A crispy and syrupy jalebi with a perfect balance of sweetness. The jalebi is fried to a delightful crunch, and the sugar syrup is not overly sweet, making it a delightful treat.

Gulab Jamun.name: Gulab Jamun
Gulab Jamun.summary: A dense and flavorful gulab jamun with a hint of saffron and a pistachio stuffing. Unlike the softer varieties, this gulab jamun has a slightly coarse texture, offering a unique take on the classic dessert.

Lassi.name: Lassi
Lassi.summary: A refreshing and not-too-thick lassi with a subtle rose water aroma. The addition of kewra (pandanus flower essence) and rose water helps to balance the sweetness, making it a perfect accompaniment to the meal.

https://goo.gl/maps/3gNsnCMSfY5MAqj78.summary: This video is a food review of Panditji Ras Bana Rahe, a street food stall in Indiranagar, Bengaluru. The stall serves North Indian, Uttar Pradesh style vegetarian food. The reviewer tries a variety of dishes, including dal poori, methi poori, aloo wadi ki subzi, chana, samosa, kachori, jalebi, gulab jamun, and lassi.  He finds the food to be delicious and authentic, with a good balance of flavors and spices. He especially enjoys the kachori, which he says is one of the best he's ever had. The reviewer also appreciates the stall's clean and hygienic environment.  The unique highlight of the restaurant is its use of mustard oil and coarse lentils in the kachori, lending it a distinct flavor and setting it apart from other kachoris.

In this quick evening stop, I made quick work of some of the must-try dishes on their menu, scrumptious samosas, a weighty, comforting dal and methi (fenugreek) poori, aloo mangodi, fresh ghee jalebis, an utterly 'khasta' kachori and more. rajanna military hotel, magadi road, vijayanagar, village style eatery, naati oota, kaima unde, mutton mince balls, mutton kurma, sambar, boti, west bengaluru, bangalore, west bangalore, bangalore food tour, eating out in bengaluru, support local, support small business

After picking up recipes from a stint in a Maratha military hotel kitchen in Bengaluru, Rajanna, a native of Kunigal, began serving non vegetarian meals in a small shed off Magadi Road in Vijayanagar 36 years ago. The menu comprised only nine items, mostly mutton, cooked by Rajanna himself with a single masala that would be ground by him at home. He passed on shortly after, but his wife and brother in law have continued his work over decades, preserving the flavour and character of the food. From a shed, it is now a tiny eatery, sans any name board, where customers queue up for rustic, village style fare served on banana leaves off granite slabs that serve as benches and tables. A recent addition also includes a basic but functional family room. I caught up with my chef friend, Sushil Dwarkanath to explore the cooking here and also make a tasty meal of their mutton delicacies. If you love meaty, rustic flavours, this is the place to savour it.

Established 36 years ago, this eatery, run by Mr. Lakshman, who inherited the legacy from his late brother-in-law, offers a rustic and authentic dining experience. Known for its traditional non-vegetarian Karnataka cuisine, the highlight of Rajanna Military Hotel is its commitment to using age-old recipes and techniques. From grinding their masalas to cleaning the meat meticulously, every step is a testament to their dedication to preserving the authenticity of the flavors.  The mutton dishes, especially the Mutton Kaima Unde, are a must-try.  The video provides a glimpse into the simple yet flavorful dishes served on granite slabs in a homely setting.  The emphasis on fresh ingredients and traditional cooking methods makes this eatery a true culinary gem.  A visit to Rajanna Military Hotel is not just a meal, it's an experience of Karnataka's rich culinary heritage.

When Gautham Reddy, a DJ, and his wife, Christine, a pastry chef, suddenly found themselves out of work due to the pandemic, they put together their savings into a culinary enterprise, a café, that met with limited success. Lesson learnt, they turned next to a home delivery business focused on non vegetarian fare derived from family recipes. Orders followed, giving them the confidence to set up a tiny eatery in the suburb of Vidyaranyapura. Things have been slow though, and when they reached out to us to help spread the word, we stepped in for a surprise visit one Wednesday afternoon. Manned by an all-women team, the fare here is the sort that is homely, tasty and most importantly, honestly priced. We tasted around 10 dishes, the sort that would happily feed a hungry party of four, and worked up a bill of just over Rs. 1200. I hope you have the heart to support enterprises like these that are committed to honest work, and trying to do their best to stay afloat in these trying times.

Mutton Kaima Fry.name: Mutton Kaima Fry
Mutton Kaima Fry.summary: This dish features coarsely ground keema that holds onto the flavors of spices and ingredients. The keema is cooked with peas, coriander, and a blend of spices, giving it a salty edge and a hint of fenugreek. The keema is sticky, indicating a good amount of mutton fat, which enhances the flavor.

Chicken Pakoda.name: Chicken Pakoda
Chicken Pakoda.summary: This dish features a thick, spiced batter that coats the chicken, adding flavor and moisture. The batter is made with roasted gram flour and green chili, giving it a spicy kick. The chicken is juicy and flavorful, making it a perfect blend of texture and taste.

Mutton Biryani.name: Mutton Biryani
Mutton Biryani.summary: This dish features tender mutton with a smoky flavor that permeates the rice. The mutton is juicy, thanks to the flavorful fat. The biryani has a subtle peppery edge and a noticeable flavor of tuppa, enhancing the overall taste.

https://goo.gl/maps/p4aUkgUkjf4xXsis7.summary: Reddy Mane Biryani, a small eatery in Vidyaranyapura, Bangalore, is a family-run business started by a DJ and his pastry chef wife after losing their jobs during the pandemic. This eatery prides itself on its home-style non-vegetarian fare, particularly its biryanis. The all-women team ensures the kitchen's hygiene and delivers fresh, home-style food.  They use family recipes and source high-quality ingredients, like the 7-8kg lamb used in their biryani.  The highlight is their dedication to maintaining the authenticity of flavors, using specific spice blends for chicken and mutton dishes. The couple's commitment to quality, home-style flavors, and affordable prices shines through, making it a must-try for anyone seeking authentic and delicious biryani.

Over 30 years ago, Dinesh Sood and his brother Deepak Sood, originally from Ludhiana, set up a tiny four-table eatery in the old market area of Balepet, Bengaluru to serve North Indian khaana to traders and travellers who would visit the area. Gaining popularity over time, Punjabi Pure Veg moved to a slightly larger first floor nook eventually, where it still stands 28 years on. The ambience, service and the decor is rather basic, but it is the rustic flavours of the food dished out by second generation owner, Aman Sood and his motley retinue of cooks that seems to hold sway over regular patrons. Also, the fact that the fare is delightfully cheap further adds to its draw. Hope you enjoy this one, visit here only for the food, nothing else.

Take care; stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

Dal Tadka.summary: A simple yet flavourful lentil dish with a tadka of onions, tomatoes, and spices. A comforting and delicious option.

Dal Makhani.summary: The creamy and rich dal makhani, slow-cooked overnight, is a must-try. It's packed with flavor and perfect with naan or kulcha.

Amritsari Naan.summary: Stuffed with a flavorful mix of mashed vegetables, including potatoes, cauliflower, paneer, and spices. This naan is a meal in itself.

Lachha Parantha.summary: Made with wheat flour, this layered parantha is crispy and flaky. It's perfect for scooping up curries or enjoying with a dollop of butter.

Tandoori Kheer.summary: A unique dessert with a smoky flavor, the tandoori kheer is a must-try. It's made with rice, milk, and sugar, slow-cooked in the residual heat of the tandoor.

Yellow Dal.summary: This homestyle yellow dal is comforting and packed with flavor. It's perfectly seasoned and best enjoyed with rice or roti.

https://g.page/punjabi-pure-veg-resturan.summary: This hidden gem in the bylanes of Chickpet, Bengaluru, has been serving authentic Amritsari cuisine for over 28 years.  Run by Aman Sood, whose family hails from Ludhiana, this no-frills eatery focuses on delivering rustic flavors at incredibly affordable prices. The highlight is their use of a flavourful 'tadka' - a tempering of onions, garlic, tomatoes, and spices - added generously to most dishes.  While the ambiance is basic, the food, especially the dals, are a must-try.  The portions are generous, making it perfect for sharing.  Arrive by metro or auto as parking is limited.

I was recently invited to a delicious initiative spearheaded by the Department of Hotel Management at Christ University, Bengaluru, where students operate an Indian restaurant every Friday. I went in expecting, well, the sort of meal that would be cooked by chefs in learning, but was simply blown away by the depth and sheer variety of traditional dishes that these young students had prepared from scratch to their mother’s recipes. The video features a visit to the Experiential Learning Restaurant (ELR) at Christ University's Department of Hotel Management in Bengaluru. Run entirely by students, the restaurant offers a unique dining experience featuring authentic Indian cuisine. On this particular Friday, the students showcase their skills with a special Mother Cuisine theme, preparing traditional dishes from the Naidu, Mudaliar, and Uttar Pradesh regions.  The host is impressed by the variety and depth of flavors in each dish, highlighting the use of fresh ingredients and traditional cooking techniques. The ELR offers a glimpse into the future of Indian cuisine, where young chefs are passionate about preserving and showcasing their culinary heritage.  
Highlight: What sets this restaurant apart is its commitment to providing students with hands-on experience in a real-world setting. The students are responsible for all aspects of the dining experience, from menu planning and food preparation to service and customer interaction, making it a truly immersive learning environment.

A couple of years ago, I had visited Kumar, a trained chef, who had turned his passion for omelets into an interesting enterprise, Egg Factor, where he would dish up gourmet ‘eggy’ creations out of a tiny stall in HSR Layout, South Bengaluru. Soon after the video was released, customers turned up in plenty to support him and it looked like nothing could go wrong. Until he arrived one morning to find his streetside eatery demolished without notice, and to make matters worse, the pandemic followed soon after. Today, Kumar and his wife, Rajalakshmi are once again trying to rebuild their lives and their small omelet  business with a borrowed push cart that is parked outside a supportive store. Hope you enjoy this episode. Do try your best to support fledgling businesses like this that are going through tough times. Take care, stay safe and strong. Happy eating!


Note: each omelet is made of four eggs and can easily serve two, or perhaps even three people with modest appetites. Please keep this in mind when considering prices here.

Having worked in Mumbai to learn the quintessential Mumbai street food, vada pav and pav bhaji, Lakshminarayan moved back to Bengaluru to set up a small eatery, Sri Ganesha Bombay Vada Pav Stores 15 years ago. Located on a busy street in Seshadripuram, North Bengaluru, this store seems to have built a tasty reputation for itself over the years catering to the neighbourhood's pandering for Mumbai style street food. I drop into this eatery to taste the vada pav, a kutchi dabeli, samosa, and the erstwhile Mumbai mill worker staple, pav bhaji. https://g.page/jagli-tindi?share.title: JAGLI TINDI | This Couple Is Reviving Traditional DAKSHINA KANNADA TIFFIN After Giving Up MNC Jobs!
https://g.page/jagli-tindi?share.description:
#vegetarian #tiffin #bangalore

traditional vegetarian snacks from south canara, mangalore, kundapura in bengaluru, jagli tindi, jagli masala dosa, kotte kadubu, kolkatte, banana kesari bath, mandakki upakari, inspiring stories, couple goals, banashankari, south bengaluru 

An engineer and mba by education respectively, Raksha Prasad and Suhas Karanth began making plans to open an eatery that would serve traditional vegetarian tiffin of their native South Canara, during their courting days. Shortly after getting married, they gave up their MNC jobs and their eatery, Jagli Tindi was born, in a tiny nook in Kengeri, on the outskirts of Bengaluru, with a menu comprising mostly dishes gleaned from their grandma’s recipes, with ingredients sourced from Kundapura to lend authenticity to the taste. Two years on, this passion enterprise has moved to a slightly larger space in Banashankari, South Bengaluru, but the couple still remain hands-on, Suhas, in the kitchen, and Raksha managing the front of the house. I visit them to learn of their inspiring story, catch some of the action in the kitchen, before sitting down to a slightly indulgent tiffin session. Hope you enjoy this episode. Stay safe and happy eating!
 
Mandakki Upakari
Made with a red puffed rice that’s tossed with their ‘secret’ podi mix and onions, topped with grated coconut and plenty of peanuts. This is the sort of fun snack that one should share with friends whilst you wait for some of the other substantial tiffin items.
Rs. 30 (usd 0.4)
8/10

Kotte Kadubu 
The kotte kadubu here is made the traditional way, steamed in cups fashioned of jackfruit leaves that lends the kadubu a distinct aroma. There’s a hint of tartness from the fermentation, the red tomato chutney makes for a sprightly partner to the gentle flavoured kadubu, with its tangy, slightly spice, sour and nutty character. The vegetable sagu adds to the nutritional quotient of this tasty tiffin.
Rs. 25 (usd 0.3)
9/10

Jagli Masala Dosa
This creation of Suhas Karanth seems to be inspired by the 99-variety dosa ilk. The dosa is smeared with a paste of potatoes, spicy podi and ghee, as it is roasted to a crisp on the tava. Folded, flattened and cut into two, this dosa creation makes for an interesting snack if you are the sort who is acquiesce to pushing the envelope for what a masala dosa can be.   
Rs. 58 (usd 0.8)
8.5/10

Kolkatte
Steamed in a banana leaf, this steamed dumpling of urad dal batter, is stained lightly with the colour of the leaf. Slightly pasty and dense in its texture, and studded with whole peppercorns that lend their tingling touch. Whilst the red chutney adds zing, next time, I would also ask for some of the nutritious vegetable saagu to complement the austerity of this steamed dumpling.
Rs. 25 (usd 0.3)
8.5/10

Banana Kesari Bath
The ripe banana heroes this velvety-textured dish from the start to finish, definitely order a plate of this to close your tindi experience here.
Rs. 25 (usd 0.3)
9/10

Coffee
Rs. 10 (usd 0.1)
8/10

Originally from Satna in Madhya Pradesh and raised in Bengaluru, Jawahar Lal always dreamt of being an entrepreneur when he worked as a North Indian cook in eateries in Bengaluru. A friend pointed him to a tiny shop on Berlie Street in Langford Town, and thus began Sudha Chaats, named after his wife, 39 years ago, to introduce Bengaluru to the joys of khasta (crisp) samosas and kachoris. The couple would cook and serve their fare piping hot; alongside the North Indian treats, their masala vada, bhajji and bonda, made interestingly with samosa stuffing, too found much favour, making their shop a popular cornerstone of the neighbourhood over time. Jawahar Lal passed on two years ago, but the tradition continues with his wife, now joined by their son, Satya Narayan. Hope you enjoy this chatpata episode. Known as the macher rani, or the queen of fish, the hilsa, or ilish, is a prized monsoon delicacy for Bengalis. And when I learnt from Chef Subhankar Dhar about a hilsa festival underway at his restaurant, Esplanade, with prized specimens of the fish caught in the Padma river of Bangladesh, which incidentally is where most of the fish originate, I wasted no time in meeting him. We caught up over a delicious repast of hilsa dishes, an insightful introduction to this prized fish, and a showcase of Bengali cuisine’s delightful nuances. Hope you enjoy this episode as much as I did. Take care, stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

https://goo.gl/maps/NwHYhKqAysHCFd8o9.summary: This video is a culinary journey through the hilsa fish festival at Esplanade, Bengaluru. The host, Kripal Amanna, along with Chef Subhankar Dhar, explore the nuances of Bengali cuisine with a focus on the prized hilsa fish.  The video highlights the cultural significance of hilsa in Bengali cuisine, its preparation techniques, and the unique flavors of each dish. From the crispy fried Ilish Mach Bhaja to the delicately steamed Bhapa Ilish, each dish showcases the versatility of this fish. The use of mustard oil, mustard paste, and traditional Bengali spices is prominent throughout the video. The highlight of the video is the emphasis on the simplicity and authenticity of Bengali flavors, highlighting the minimal use of ingredients to let the taste of the hilsa shine through. The video is a celebration of Bengali food and culture, offering viewers an immersive experience through vivid descriptions and visuals.

#BengaliFood #Bangalore #GourmetOnTheRoad 

Esplanade, Authentic Bengali Restaurant, Indiranagar, Bengaluru. Recipes from Chef Subhankar Dhar’s Mother. Best Bengali Restaurant in Bangalore, shuktoni, begun bhaja, bhetki paturi, daab chingri, katla jhol, kasha mangsho, mishit doi, rosogolla

Esplanade has been catering to Bengali palates in Bengaluru for the last 12 years. Helmed by Chef Subhankar Dhar, a native of Kolkata, it is the destination to savour an authentic Bengali meal experience in an elegant setting.

In this episode of Gourmet On The Road, Food Lovers’ Editor catches up with Chef Dhar before settling down to a sumptuous meal that covers the entire spectrum of a Bengali lunch - from shukto to dal to bhaja to paturi, jhol, mangsho and chutney before ending with mishti, desserts. Enjoy! 

SHUKTONI 
The traditional way to start a Bengali lunch, the Shuktoni, made with cow’s milk, sun dried lentil dumplings and flavoured with wild celery seeds, radhuni, is rich in vegetables. 
Rs. 195 (usd 2.7)
9/10

BHAJA MUNGER DAL
This is a comforting lentil dish, mellow in its flavours, embellished with fresh peas and hint of cumin in its ghee seasoning. 
Rs. 185 (usd 2.6)
8/10

BEGUN BHAJA 
Thick, fleshy slices of eggplant, roasted on a tawa. The pulpy ‘begun’ has a sweetish edge contrasted by the slightly bitter tones of its skin. A
Rs. 175 (usd 2.5) for 4 pcs
9/10

JHUE JHUREE ALOO BHAJA 
Rs. 155 (usd 2.2)
7/10

DHOKAR DALNA 
Lentil, gram flour cakes simmered in a spicy tomato onion gravy. The stodgy texture of the dhokar is lifted by the spirited flavours of the spicy gravy, dalna. 
Rs. 235 (usd 3.3)
8/10

BHETKI PATURI
This dish is an ode to the Bengali palate’s fascination with mustard. The Kolkata bhetki is swathed in a paste of mustard, coconut and green chillies, wrapped in a banana leaf and roasted, rendering the fish firm to the touch but moist inside. Rs. 475 (usd 6.7)

9/10

DAAB CHINGRI 
The sweetness of the coconut milk and tender coconut, the punch of mustard, the grainy texture of poppy seeds and the heat from green chillies come together to make this flavourful curry.  
Rs. 595 (usd 8.3)
8.5/10

KATLA JHOL
The plump piece of katla, a pond fish, is fried first before being introduced to the curry which has a lilt of fennel in its flavours. The fish is earthy in its aroma, has a bit of a bite around the edges and its soft and fleshy texture is the perfect medium to soak up the flavours of the jhol. 
Rs. 395 (usd 5.5)
10/10

KASHA MANGSHO 
A slow cooked dish of onions and meat in equal measure, braised over four hours, the kasha mangsho epitomises ‘meaty indulgence’! The fat, gelatin and marrow of the meat lend to the savoury, unctuous character of the dark, braised onions. Rs. 495 (usd 7)
10/10

TOMATO KHEJUR CHUTNEY
Rs. 95 (usd 1.3)
8/10

MISHTI DOI 
Flavoured with seasonal, nolen or nutan, meaning ‘new’, gur, jaggery tapped from the date palm, this is a lush, sweet end to the meal at Esplanade. 
Rs. 145 (usd 2)
9/10

BAKED ROSOGOLLA 
Rosogolla made with nolen gur, soaked in a sugar-nolen gur syrup, topped with a nolen gur enriched reduced milk before being baked, this mishti screams decadent indulgence. 
Rs. 195 (usd 2.7)
8/10

best_dishes.name: Misal
best_dishes.summary: A hearty and flavorful dish with a mix of textures and spices. It features matki (moth bean), semolina, onions, tomatoes, and a special blend of spices. To enhance the flavors, ask for their rasa (a flavorful gravy) on the side.

best_dishes.name: Masala Khara
best_dishes.summary: A delightful medley of flavors and textures, this dish will tantalize your taste buds. It's a combination of chuda (beaten rice), mixture, onions, tomatoes, lime, sugar, and a hint of spice. The masala khara offers a perfect balance of sweetness, sourness, and crunch.

best_dishes.name: Bread Toast
best_dishes.summary: This unique dish features thick bread slathered with ghee and topped with masala potato filling. Served with onion palya and chutney, it offers a blend of sweet, savory, and spicy flavors. While it might be an acquired taste, the bread toast is a local favorite.

best_dishes.name: Bonda Soup
best_dishes.summary: A light and flavorful soup with a delicate blend of spices. It has a base of lentils and vegetables, enhanced with aromatic cumin, coconut, and a hint of green chili. This soup is a perfect example of how simple ingredients can create a delicious and comforting dish.

When Mr Vasudev Shetty moved from Mangalore to Hubli to begin Gurudatta Bhavan in 1958, he may not have imagined that in times to come his eatery would become one of the most popular food destinations in this bustling commercial hub. Be it breakfast, lunch or dinner, Gurudatta Bhavan seems to draw in the denizens of Hubballi in numbers for its tasty fare that blends Mangalorean culinary style with influences of the land. Eshwar Rao entered the kitchen of a generations-old military hotel when he was barely into his teens. It was here that he learnt age-old Karnataka-Maratha recipes from his mentor, Rukmini Bai over decades of diligent labor, that he now serves up in his rustic eatery, S G Rao’s Military Hotel in Cottonpet, Bengaluru. I met this entrepreneur, now in his forties, and caught the making of a unique military style pulav, in addition to a tasting of some of the other must-haves here. The pulav here is cooked only with the gravy of the meat, the meat that is then layered under the rice just before serving. And interestingly, the chicken pulav too is cooked in any mutton gravy that may be available! Hope you enjoy this tasty episode. Take care; stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

OG Variar & Sons Bakery, popularly known as Variar Bakery, traces its roots to 1954 when O Govinda Variar, a native of Kannur, Kerala, set up a small bakery in Guttahalli, Northwest Bengaluru, selling breads and buns. Eventually he moved to Rajajinagar in 1970 before opening a second bakery on Chord Road, West Bengaluru. What makes Variar bakery immensely popular with locals is its philosophy that “excludes artificial additives, preservatives and chemically bleached flour in its vast range of baked products.” As a result, “there is no shining in our items,” says second generation owner, Vijaya Shankar, who is currently on a quest to substitute, to the extent possible, detrimental fats with healthier options of unrefined oil, ghee, butter across most of their range, and in certain products, maida with wholewheat flour and grains. I spent the better part of a day exploring the bakery and tasting many of the must-haves at this institution that has spawned many imitators. OG Variar & Sons Bakery, popularly known as Variar Bakery, traces its roots to 1954 when O Govinda Variar, a native of Kannur, Kerala, set up a small bakery in Guttahalli, Northwest Bengaluru, selling breads and buns. Eventually he moved to Rajajinagar in 1970 before opening a second bakery on Chord Road, West Bengaluru. What makes Variar bakery immensely popular with locals is its philosophy that “excludes artificial additives, preservatives and chemically bleached flour in its vast range of baked products.” As a result, “there is no shining in our items,” says second generation owner, Vijaya Shankar, who is currently on a quest to substitute, to the extent possible, detrimental fats with healthier options of unrefined oil, ghee, butter across most of their range, and in certain products, maida with wholewheat flour and grains. I spent the better part of a day exploring the bakery and tasting many of the must-haves at this institution that has spawned many imitators. Chonak (White Snapper) Tava Fry.summary: The masala balances perfectly against the fleshy character of the fish. The fish is moist and the masala complements the fish well. The masala has chili, turmeric and salt.

Kalwa (Oyster) Rava Fry.summary: Dominated by the flavor of the oysters. Briny notes and slightly metallic in flavor. The masala is nicely seasoned with chili, turmeric, salt and you can taste the inner sweet flavors of the oyster.

Shinane (Mussels) rava fry.summary: You can taste more of the rava than the mussels. There is a bit of a salty hit from the batter. The crunchy texture of the rava and the briny flavors of the mussels make a good combination.

Tisryo (Clams) sukka.summary: A bit of a sandy flavor. There is a fair bit of chili heat in the masala. The masala is a little more liquidy.

Drumstick Prawn curry.summary: The prawns are tiny and packed with a lot of flavor. The curry is sour and spicy, the heat grips your tongue. Best to have it with drumsticks.

Some of the must-try dishes include the Chonak Tava Fry, Kalwa (Oyster) Rava Fry,  Drumstick Prawn curry and Tisryo (Clams) sukka.  The restaurant is run by the son of the owner who passed away a year ago. The restaurant is popular for its seafood and is frequented by locals.

kesaramadu tumkur idli hotel, gangadhar idli hotel kesaramadu, tumkur, ghee roast idli, thatte idli, mini masala dosae,  tumkur kesarmadu hotel, kesaramadu roasted idli, kyathasandra, bangalore highway, nh 48, highway restaurant, bengaluru davanagere highway, idli, vegetarian, village breakfast, breakfast, snack, karnataka, support local, support small business

Gangadhar, real name Krishnamurthy, is a man who wears many hats - former president of the gram panchayat, farmer and eatery owner. It is the last hat though that is relevant here. 16 years ago, he set up a makeshift shed to serve the famous Kyathasandra thatte Idli but away from the bustle of the main Tumkur highway, on a narrow village road leading to a tiny hamlet, Kesaramadu. Slowly but surely the popularity of his solitary village eatery grew for its thatte Idli, dosae and simple rustic lunch that came as a boon to the farming folks around. However, four years ago some customers recommended that he try roasting the Idli in ghee, and thus was born his, now-referred-to-as, Kesaramadu Roast Idli. Thatte idlis are steamed, cooled and then slow roasted on a dosae tawa with liberal lashings of ghee. Ten minutes later, the idlis take on a delicious, buttery crust that sends the palate into raptures brought on by molten streams of ghee. And it is this idli that seems to have put Gangadhar Idli Hotel, Kesaramadu, on the food lovers map! Hope you enjoy this rustic breakfast episode. Take care; stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

Despite facing initial resistance to the idea from her father, she persisted, and finally after convincing her family for over six months, Zamindar Restaurant finally opened in HRBR Layout, East Bengaluru, with a menu repertoire that paid homage to her Andhra roots, biryanis, and spanning other cuisine influences to cater to Bengaluru’s cosmopolitan diners. In a relatively short span of under four years, her restaurant has carved out a significant niche for itself with its offerings that are built around the promise of “tasty fare at prices that offer maximum value”. A trained pastry chef by profession, Kennedy Dias worked many years overseas crafting fine cakes and pastries. However, he yearned to be back home in Caranzalem, Goa. He finally returned and mustered the courage to set up a cake shop but “people didn’t understand fine pastries 20 years ago”, he says. So, after a couple of unsuccessful years, he began making puffs, pies and chops, the sort of traditional fare that locals appreciate and love. And along the way experimented with a home-smoked curry-leaf infused Goan sausage, that is now a must-try here. Since then, his tiny shop has become much popular with the locals and young students for his omelets, sandwiches, burgers, pies and interesting shakes and juices. This is the sort of honest dive that one should also visit for a true taste of small town Goa, away from the tourist trail.

Located in the heart of Panjim, Kokni Kanteen seeks to introduce guests to the Kokni, or traditional Saraswat cuisine of Goa,  in a format that is friendly and comfortable. Fitting when one learns that the bungalow it is housed in dates back to Portuguese rule and served as an inn where locals would be fed when they traveled from the villages. I step in here to savour a reasonably priced viswon (kingfish) thali and an interesting array of flavourful GSB preparations, both vegetarian and non vegetarian, that are rarely found outside homes. What began as a local haunt has now evolved to a destination where visitors can help themselves to a delicious serving of Goa’s rich and varied cuisines. Hope you enjoy this episode; take care, stay safe and strong. Happy eating.

enne khaara mutton, chicken, hotel nartaki, family run eatery, ranebennur, sappey mutton, chicken sukka, mutton chops, boti, khuska, non vegetarian eatery, north karnataka, highway eatery, karnataka food tour, north karnataka food tour, karnataka tourism, north karnataka cuisine, support local

I had heard much about this very special Ranebennur mutton preparation, the enne  khara, translating literally to oil and chilli heat, drawing from its two principal ingredients. And so on our recent drive to Goa, we planned a lunch stop in this agricultural town in North Karnataka at Hotel Nartaki, the home of this iconic dish. Established 30 years ago by N Satish, a tailor turned restaurateur, in a tiny eatery that could only accommodate a few customers at a time. His wife would help him make the masala at home that he would cook into curries. Along the way, he came up with the concept of enne khaara largely to appease the spice-hungry tastebuds of the locals. The dish, in contrast to its fiery name, is a beautiful balance of flavours between the chilli heat (from a combination of 90% local Javannur chillies that also impart a striking colour to the dish, and 10% Guntur chillies) and the oil that rounds off all the sharp edges of the masala aided by the sourness of tomatoes. Mr N Satish has since passed on but the homemade tradition continues with his sons, Chetan and Chandan, in a much larger space today, aided by their mother and wives. If you love your meaty fare, Hotel Nartaki is certainly worth a visit, I would say even a detour should you be travelling in the area. I hope you enjoy this very special episode. Take care, stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

I heard from a few locals that this unassuming roadside eatery on Parra Main Road, North Goa, serves a xacuti that was worth the 20 odd kilometer drive from where we were staying in Dona Paula. But when we arrived, the chicken xacuti was over as were some other popular breakfast eats like egg chops, etc.. Nonetheless, we stepped into the kitchen to check what was available and found the remnants of a xacuti gravy that owner, Mahesh Parsekar’s mother prepares at home. The roasted spice aroma of the gravy was enticing, and so when Mahesh offered to cook a ros omelet with the gravy, I knew we had to try it. The weighty omelet was elevated a few notches by the aromatic flavours of the xacuti, and I definitely look forward to returning to Sai Anant Parra someday in the hope of tasting more of the traditional home cooked fare. Hope you enjoy this short vlog on a hidden Goa gem. Happy eating; take care, stay safe and strong.

While the chicken Xacuti ran out early, we were lucky to savor the remaining gravy's magic in a delectable Ros Omelet. The dish, a testament to the owner's mother's culinary prowess, impressed with its aromatic spices and the depth of flavor infused into every bite.  Sai Anant, a hidden gem, promises a delightful experience for food enthusiasts seeking authentic Goan flavors. What makes it unique is that the Xacuti masala, a blend of 36 ingredients, is prepared at the owner's home, adding a touch of home-cooked goodness to the dishes.

If you want to savour delicious Goan Catholic culinary traditions, Bhatti Village, a quaint home turned restaurant amidst the lush fields of Bhatti Waddo in Nerul, is where you need to be. Run by the D'Souza family, the food here is the sort that you would taste in a Goan home if they were blessed with an extraordinary cook. The flavours are punchy and the hospitality of the family, warming, and the sort that immerses one in the conviviality of Goa’s people. A reason why this charming home eatery has endeared itself to locals and travellers for over 25 years. In this dinner episode, I met the family and also made myself comfortable with a large meal in which almost  every dish had me licking my fingers! 😋

https://g.page/bhatti-village-family-bar.summary: Tucked away in the lush fields of Bhatti Waddo in Nerul, Goa,  Bhatti Village is not just a restaurant but a culinary haven for Goan Catholic cuisine enthusiasts. Run by the warm and welcoming D'Souza family, this 25-year-old establishment, once their humble abode, promises an authentic Goan home-style dining experience.  What sets Bhatti Village apart is its commitment to tradition, evident in its no-menu policy and dishes prepared using local ingredients and age-old recipes. You'll be spoilt for choice with their array of seafood specialties, their signature pork sorpotel, and the legendary Serradura. A highlight of Bhatti Village is their use of locally brewed cashew feni, adding a touch of local flavor.  A meal at Bhatti Village is more than just food; it's an immersion into the heart of Goan culture and hospitality.

An acclaimed Yakshagana artist, Prabhakara Upadhyay began Saligrama’s Mantap Ice Cream in Bengaluru in 1981 when he realized the need for a business to earn a livelihood. In those days, the denizens of (then) chilly Bangalore were hesitant to eat ice creams afraid they may fall ill, and thus began a long and arduous journey of educating people to appreciate and enjoy these frozen treats. The effort seems to have paid off over the years, making this vegetarian ice cream parlour a household name amongst old Bangaloreans. From multiple outlets, Mantap has now scaled back to only one store in Seshadripuram, where Mantapa Upadhyay, (as he is popularly known) dreams up combinations that he personally puts together each morning with dairy rich ice creams that are sourced from a premium ice cream supplier. In this conversation with him and his family, I savour a range of his delectable creations - from traditional pure organic jaggery, guava chilli, to inspirations like the fruit fusion, red velvet cake, and classics like rich mango cream and caramel, and a couple of delicious faloodas too. This store is a definite must-visit if you love ice cream.

46 years ago, Rohidas Desai took over an existing taverna off Eduarte Pacheco street in Panjim to set up his seafood restaurant. Fastidious about the quality of seafood, he would visit the market each day to scour for the best marine produce to be cooked to his wife, Gokula Desai’s recipes. It is no surprise then that this committed approach had earned for Ritz legions of ardent patrons who now pack the group's six restaurants for lunch and dinner. I caught up with Daad (as he is known to everyone in Goa) Desai in a meeting that was ordained by destiny over a seafood lunch at their very first eatery, Café Ritz. Hope you enjoy this episode; take care, stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

For the best traditional Goan desserts and scrumptious savoury treats, locals swear by Mr. Baker, a 100-year-old institution that remains steadfast to its culinary roots. I met with third generation owner, Nenette Fernandes, over a leisurely tasting of bebinca, battica, risoi, croquettes, the sort of baked wares that even her grandfather, Mr. Pedro Vincent Vaz who founded the bakery, would recognise if he were around today. The video highlights the unique and gentle flavors of Goan vegetarian cuisine, showcasing dishes like Tamata Bhaji, Sukhi Bhaji, Alsanna Bhaji, and their special Goan Samosa.  The reviewer emphasizes the heartwarming atmosphere of the café, where people come not just for the food but also for the conversations and connections.  The video offers a glimpse into the heart of Goan culture, where food and community intertwine to create a memorable experience.

popular bajji shop in jayanagar, south bangalore, vegetable, pakora, bonda, capsicum masala bajji, aloo bonda, potato, mirchi bajji, street food, jayanagar, 4th block jayanagar, jayanagar street food, bengaluru, vegetarian eatery, bangalore food trail, karnataka food tour, support local, support small business

Krishna Poojary migrated from his hometown in Kundapura to Bengaluru nearly half a century ago in search of a livelihood. After a string of odd jobs in eateries, he decided to try his hand at a bajji (fried fritter) gaadi (cart) in Jayanagar 4th block, Bengaluru. It’s been 42 years since; the location of his cart has changed from one street to another over the years, but the place that his fried wares occupy in the hearts and palates of his neighbourhood patrons remains constant to this day. Also perhaps making Kundapura Bonda Bajji Shop one of the area's oldest street food carts! I visited him one cloudy Bengaluru evening to taste all the bondas and bajjis he and his son have on offer. 

Hope you enjoy this episode in our ongoing initiative to support small businesses, do support your neighbourhood eateries too. Take care; stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

kaleels kitchen, homely seafood restaurant, mudigere, spice town, hassan charmadi highway, seafood lunch, traditional fish curry, fish fry, prawn ghee roast, squid masala, anjal fry, bangda masala fry, mackerel fry, pullimunchi, mangalorean cuisine, food trail, karnataka food tour, support local, support small business

On my last drive through the Western ghats into Mangalore, I stopped for lunch in the spice town of Mudigere, around 80 kilometres from Hassan, at an old bungalow converted into a cosy eatery. It was here that I met an incredibly hard working brother-sister duo. Kaleel makes a 240 kilometer return trip every other night to procure fresh seafood from the fishing harbour in Mangalore, that his sister Arshia single handedly cooks to family recipes. The flavours of the homely fare here is reminiscent of what you would taste in kudla (Mangalore)  but with the sort of punchy spicing that they say “is suited to the local palate of Mudigere”. I enjoyed my meal at Kaleel’s Kitchen, hope you relish this episode too. Take care; stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

gavran misal, hsr layout, bengaluru, south bengaluru, authentic misal pav, kolhapuri misal, vada pav, rural, maharashtrian cuisine, street food, vegetarian snacks,  gavran misal recipe, gavran misal cooking, vegetarian eatery, bengaluru, bangalore food trail, karnataka food tour, support local, support small business

Sujit Lakade missed Kolhapuri Misal Pav when he moved to Bengaluru a few years ago. In this he saw an opportunity to showcase to Bengaluru the village rendition of this quintessential Maharashtrian street food staple, an approach that conveys delicious, spicy flavours with minimal fuss. And so Gavran Misal was born, with ingredients sourced from Kolhapur, given his family’s lineage in the food grains business. Here, the tari, the spicy rasa (gravy) at the heart of the dish, is cooked over a wood fire, thereby also imbuing this modest eatery, with a rustic smokey appeal, where regulars wolf down the misal pav and vada pav, the only two items served here in addition to kokum and taak (buttermilk) to wash things down. 

If you’re looking to savour some authentic rural flavours, head here. Hope you enjoy this episode. Take care; stay safe and strong. Happy eating!
