Misal Pav.name: Misal Pav
Misal Pav.summary: A spicy and flavorful curry made with moth beans, potatoes, and spices, served with pav (bread). The misal is cooked on a wood fire, giving it a unique smoky flavor. Customers can customize their misal by adding more onions, kat (spicy oil), or rasa (curry).

Vada Pav.name: Vada Pav
Vada Pav.summary: A crispy potato patty served in a soft and fluffy pav (bread) with garlic chutney and fried green chilies. The vada pav is not very spicy but has a nice crunch and flavor.

https://goo.gl/maps/mmN3yXnMhG1GesJ97.summary: Gavran Misal in Bengaluru, owned by Sujit Lakade, offers an authentic taste of Kolhapuri village-style cuisine.  The restaurant is known for its use of minimal ingredients and traditional cooking methods, including a wood-fired stove.  Their signature dish, Misal Pav, is a must-try, known for its spicy and flavorful curry.  The restaurant also serves Vada Pav, a popular street food snack. The rustic ambiance and the use of ingredients sourced from Kolhapur add to the authenticity of the dining experience. Gavran Misal stands out for its commitment to delivering the true flavors of Kolhapuri cuisine.

When Mr Chenna Reddy migrated from his village in Andhra Pradesh just past the Karnataka border town of Mulbagal in the eighties, he sought employment as a cook in an Andhra eatery in Bengaluru. Such was his impressive hand at cooking, that some of his customers and associates pooled together a restaurant for him, and thus was born Mayuri in 1986, just off Minerva circle on JC Road. 36 years on, the eatery still reigns supreme for its Andhra fare, notably the vegetarian bhojanam and toothsome biryanis, the latter made to a unique recipe that employs minimal spices yet makes a terrific impact on the palate! In this episode, I catch up with Mr. Reddy as he walks me through his kitchen and preparations, his unbridled passion quite inspiring, before sitting down for a big Andhra meal comprising Mayuri’s most popular hits. Hope you find this slightly lengthy episode enjoyable, well, I certainly did 😉😋. Take care; stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

https://goo.gl/maps/rzbBDFFLtAr41ov98.summary: Mayuri, located in Minerva Circle, JC Road, Bangalore, is a legendary Andhra restaurant that has been serving authentic Andhra cuisine for over 35 years.  This episode provides a glimpse into the heart of Mayuri, showcasing their most popular dishes and the passion of its founder, Mr. Chenna Reddy.  Mr. Reddy's commitment to quality and authentic flavors is evident in every dish, from the perfectly balanced Chilli Chicken to the aromatic Mutton Biryani. The highlight of Mayuri is undoubtedly their biryani, made with minimal spices but abundant flavor, a testament to their belief that less is more. A visit to Mayuri is a culinary journey back in time, where one can savor the true essence of Andhra cuisine in a nostalgic setting.

An engineer by profession, Apeksha was always interested in the food business. Backed by her husband and a friend, she took the plunge a few months ago in setting up a tiny eatery in Padmanabhanagar, South Bengaluru, where the vegetarian menu is a mix of local favourites and snack items from Dakshina Kannada. Having received a few recommendations from their patrons in the neighbourhood, I ventured out one evening to meet this young, confident entrepreneur and support her fledgling enterprise, in doing so, I taste a satisfying tiffin of idli vade served with a rather impressionable sambar, a subtly-flavoured Mangalore bun, nourishing bonda soup and some more, before rounding off my meal with an organic jaggery coffee. Idli Sambar.summary: Idli Sambar is a popular South Indian breakfast dish. It features soft and fluffy idlis served with a flavorful and aromatic sambar. The sambar at Brahmin’s Veg Corner is known for its slightly sweet and tangy flavor, with a perfect balance of spices.

Mangalore Buns.name: Mangalore Buns
Mangalore Buns.summary: Mangalore Buns are a delicious Mangalorean delicacy. These sweet and fluffy buns are made with ripe bananas, flour, and a blend of spices. Brahmin’s Veg Corner serves their Mangalore Buns with a side of coconut chutney and sambar.

Bonda Soup.name: Bonda Soup
Bonda Soup.summary: Bonda Soup is a comforting and flavorful South Indian dish. It consists of crispy and golden-brown bondas served in a flavorful and aromatic lentil soup. Brahmin’s Veg Corner prepares their Bonda Soup with a spicy and tangy dal, which complements the bondas perfectly.

Avalakki Bath.name: Avalakki Bath
Avalakki Bath.summary: Avalakki Bath is a traditional Karnataka breakfast dish. It is made with flattened rice (poha) that is cooked with vegetables, spices, and herbs. Brahmin’s Veg Corner makes a flavourful Avalakki Bath with the right amount of crunch and a balance of sweet and savory flavors.

https://goo.gl/maps/7nW69goggKE6sSgw7.summary: Brahmin’s Veg Corner is a small eatery located in a narrow bylane of Padmanabhanagar in South Bengaluru. This hidden gem is run by Apeksha, a young engineer turned entrepreneur, and her husband.  The restaurant offers a delightful vegetarian menu featuring South Indian staples and unique dishes from the Dakshina Kannada region.  The highlight of Brahmin’s Veg Corner is their Idli Vada Sambar, where the sambar steals the show with its unique sweetish flavor profile, a testament to Apeksha's culinary creativity. The Mangalore buns, a personal favorite of the host, are made with a generous amount of ripe bananas, giving them a naturally sweet flavor and soft texture. Another must-try is their Bonda Soup, where crispy bondas are generously doused in a spicy and aromatic lentil soup.  Beyond the food, the eatery has a heart-warming story.  Apeksha's passion for food and her entrepreneurial spirit are evident in every aspect of the restaurant.  The cozy ambiance and friendly service add to the overall charm of the place.  Brahmin’s Veg Corner is a true testament to the fact that sometimes, the best culinary experiences are found in the most unassuming of places.

Stepping into Sri Ram Bhavan at Ayodhya Hotel is akin to stepping back in time. Not just in terms of its decor but the dishes that are served here, many which are found rarely now, and that too mostly in homes that have managed to hold on to their culinary traditions. I drop in for breakfast and and make a big breakfast of many delicacies that I hadn’t tasted hitherto - like the patholi, a stuffed rice and jackfruit pancake steamed in banana leaf, thekre idli, an unusual steamed rice dumpling made with cucumber, a raw jackfruit roast, patrode, spiced and steamed colocasia leaves, and lots more. If you want to savour an old-fashioned South Canara breakfast, more specifically a GSB meal, this is the place to visit when in Mangalore. Hope you enjoy this episode. Take care; stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

https://goo.gl/maps/Ucjbpq6GPErz2Bdu6.summary: Sri Ram Bhavan at Ayodhya Hotel in Mangalore offers a unique dining experience with its old-world charm and rare, traditional South Canara dishes, especially GSB cuisine. The restaurant has been serving authentic flavors for 75 years and is highly recommended for its breakfast. Some of the must-try dishes include Patholi, Thekrey Idli, Patrode, Sanna Dose, and Neyyappam. The jackfruit dishes and the jaggery jalebi at the sweet shop are also worth trying. The restaurant offers delicious food at very affordable prices, making it a great value for money.

Hotel Nayak Fish Land in Murudeshwar is a popular spot for fresh seafood, especially their fish thali and tandoori preparations.  The fish curry is a standout, with a spicy and tart flavor profile that lingers on the palate. The restaurant also offers a variety of fried fish and prawn dishes, including a prawn rava fry and an anjal masala fry. The tandoori pomfret, a large and fresh fish, is marinated in a blend of mustard oil, vinegar, and spices and cooked to perfection in a tandoor, resulting in a crispy exterior and moist and flaky interior.  The restaurant's coastal location is evident in the use of kokum, a souring agent common in the region, which is served at the end of the meal to aid digestion.  If you find yourself in Murudeshwar craving seafood, Nayak Fish Land is definitely worth checking out.  
Highlight: The standout dish is the fish curry with its unique spicy and tart flavor, a must-try for anyone visiting the restaurant.

appu shet mangalore, sri mahalasa appu shet angadi, mangalore, popular egg stumbler, egg roll, bonda lime, fresh fruit, fruit juices, mangalore, south canara, 90 year old shop, mangalore food trail, karnataka food tour, support local, support small business

Dating back to 1932, Sri Mahalasa Appu Shet Shop diversified into cooking egg based dishes around three decades ago. Creations like egg stumbler, a spicy assemblage of scrambled eggs, seasoned and toasted bread dices, a moist egg roll, among others have since made it a delicious habit for the denizens of Mangalore. And what better way to cool off, both from the weather, and spicy heat, than with some seasonal fruit juices and refreshing concoctions. I visited this store, now run by the third and fourth generation of the Shet family, one warm evening to make a big meal of a couple of egg snacks, a few fruit juices and a platter of fresh fruit. Appu Shet angadi certainly merits a visit when in this port city. Hope you enjoy this episode; take care, stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

Goli Baje.name: Goli Baje
Goli Baje.summary: Deep-fried snack made from maida and urad dal batter that is left to ferment for a few hours, resulting in a slightly sour taste. It has a crispy outer layer and a soft and fluffy interior, seasoned with cumin, green chilies, and curry leaves, and best enjoyed with spicy coconut chutney.

Balehannu Podi.name: Balehannu Podi
Balehannu Podi.summary: Ripe banana slices dipped in a crispy batter flavored with carom seeds and deep-fried. The banana becomes soft and caramelized, offering a sweet and slightly sour taste, complementing the savory batter.

Special Dosae.name: Special Dosae
Special Dosae.summary: A unique dosa made with a combination of urad dal and maida, resulting in a soft and crispy texture. It is thicker than a regular dosa and has a slightly fermented flavor. The dosa is speckled with green chilies and curry leaves, adding a hint of spice, and is served with coconut chutney and sambar.

Kashi Halwa.name: Kashi Halwa
Kashi Halwa.summary: Translucent and melt-in-your-mouth halwa made from ash gourd (white pumpkin), cooked with generous amounts of sugar, ghee, and cardamom. The sweetness is balanced by a hint of sourness, and the addition of raisins adds bursts of caramelized sweetness.

Coffee.name: Coffee
Coffee.summary: A rich and aromatic coffee sourced from the renowned Panduranga Coffee in Chikmagalur. The blend, known as Grand Aroma, consists of 80% coffee and 20% chicory, offering a unique flavor profile with caramel notes.

This iconic eatery, run by the Bhat family for over six decades, is renowned for its traditional Mangalorean delicacies. Witness the art of making their signature dish, Goli Baje, a crispy and fluffy deep-fried snack. Indulge in the sweet and savory Balehannu Podi, made with ripe banana and a flavorful batter. Savour their Special Dosae, a unique and crispy dosa, and don't miss the Kashi Halwa, a melt-in-your-mouth dessert. Complete your culinary journey with their exceptional coffee, sourced from the famed Panduranga Coffee. Hotel Woodlands offers a nostalgic culinary experience that captures the essence of Mangalore's rich food culture.  A must-try for anyone seeking authentic South Indian flavors in a historic setting. The highlight of Hotel Woodlands is the dedication to tradition and the use of high-quality ingredients, evident in their signature dishes like Goli Baje and the specially sourced coffee from Panduranga Coffee, ensuring an unforgettable dining experience.

During my very first Gourmet On The Road season over a couple of years ago, I visited this brave lady entrepreneur’s food truck, Halli Mane Rottis in Mangalore. Emerging through tough circumstances, her delicious Malenadu fare was winning hearts and palates in kudla and she seemed to be doing well, also winning numerous accolades for her grit and determination. However things are far from good for Shilpa and her family currently, I discovered when I chanced upon the food truck on my last visit to the city. I learnt that the family was going through a time due to the pandemic and also that Shilpa was largely confined to her home due to a serious back problem. She cooks what she can at home aided by her brother who then sells the food out of the truck with her father. Whilst their economic situation may be dire, the food that they dish out is still as delicious as before, I relished a toothsome green chicken curry, a spicy leg piece with soft akki rotti.

I hope you find it in your heart to support enterprises like Halli Mane Rottis. Take care; stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

When their 70-year-old eatery, Hotel Lakshmi Nivas, popularly known as KT Hotel, in Kalladka was demolished to make way for a flyover construction, Shivaram Holla and his wife, Mamatha resolved to bounce back as quickly as they could. Determined to hold on to the legacy left behind by their forefathers, during this difficult time, they gathered every bit of the rubble of the old structure and poured it into the foundation of their new building that has emerged just a few steps behind the original location. And they managed to do this in just under two months! I was amazed at their incredible determination to fiercely protect the Kalladka Tea and Rimjhim Coffee  tradition that has quite literally put this town, 30 kilometers outside Mangalore on the food lovers map. Mrs Prema continues in the legacy of her father, Mr Venkateshwara, who began a tiny idli hut in a bylane of Hassan adjoining the main market area. Over time the eatery moved to a tiny shop down the road, but its main offering, the idli continues to be a crowd pleaser, even 36 years on! Over 1500 of these are steamed each morning, to a unique batter that incorporates kusubalakki, urad dal and sabakki, sago pearls, in equal proportion; the Idlis are soft and sponge-like in texture to drink up the ghee that is drizzled over. It is served with a unique onion palya that is only tempered with salt and turmeric, and a fiery red chilli chutney made of peanuts, red chillies, cumin and garlic. The decor here is nothing to speak of, just some benches strewn around a tiny shed, but it doesn't seem to deter its patrons from lining up in queues to savour piping hot idlis for only the four or five hours they are open for business every morning.

In 1969, P. Ramachandra Upadhyay, then barely in his teens, migrated from Saligrama, Udupi district, to Kanakapura to work in Vasu Hotel, an eatery famous even then for its masala dosae. This form of the dosae though was a foreign concept to Ramachandra, who coincidentally came from a small village called Parampalli, where the khali dosa was prepared as an offering to Lord Maha Vishnu. Notwithstanding his lack of knowledge, the young lad worked hard in the kitchen and in a span of 14 years was handed ownership of the Vasu Hotel by the then owners who wished to retire. Nearly 50 years on, this no-frills eatery located 50 kilometers from Bengaluru still reigns supreme, not just for its sumptuous masala dosae and other old-fashioned tiffin and sweet treats, but also for its honest approach to pricing. I caught up with Mr Upadhyay and his son, Janardhan on a trip back from Mysuru.

The host highlights the unique deep reddish-brown roast of their dosa and its robust texture that can hold a generous amount of potato filling.  He praises the balance of flavors in the dosa, chutney, and the perfectly spiced potato filling. #vasuhotel #masaladosa #kanakapura

popular masala dosae restaurant in kanakapura, karnataka, highway stop, vasu hotel kanakapura, dosae, makhmal puri, boondi ladoo, gulab jamun, filter coffee, road trip, motorcycling, 50 kilometres from bangalore, bengaluru, breakfast, tiffin, traditional, kanakapura, karnataka, karnataka food tour, support local

In 1969, P. Ramachandra Upadhyay, then barely in his teens, migrated from Saligrama, Udupi district, to Kanakapura to work in Vasu Hotel, an eatery famous even then for its masala dosae. This form of the dosae though was a foreign concept to Ramachandra, who coincidentally came from a small village called Parampalli, where the khali dosa was prepared as an offering to Lord Maha Vishnu. Notwithstanding his lack of knowledge, the young lad worked hard in the kitchen and in a span of 14 years was handed ownership of the Vasu Hotel by the then owners who wished to retire. Nearly 50 years on, this no-frills eatery located 50 kilometers from Bengaluru still reigns supreme, not just for its sumptuous masala dosae and other old-fashioned tiffin and sweet treats, but also for its honest approach to pricing. I caught up with Mr Upadhyay and his son, Janardhan on a trip back from Mysuru.

Boondi Ladoo.name: Boondi Ladoo
Boondi Ladoo.summary: A classic Indian sweet made with gram flour boondi (small, fried balls) and sugar syrup. The ladoos at Vasu Hotel have a distinct cardamom flavor and a slightly crunchy texture.

Gulab Jamun.name: Gulab Jamun
Gulab Jamun.summary: Soft, melt-in-your-mouth gulab jamuns soaked in a fragrant sugar syrup flavored with rose water. The gulab jamuns here are a delightful balance of sweet and aromatic.

Coffee.name: Coffee
Coffee.summary: Strong South Indian filter coffee, perfect for sipping after a hearty meal.

Three generations on, this military hotel, an adage used for rustic eateries that serve predominantly non vegetarian fare in parts of the South, is still run with an attitude of service by members of his family, as I discovered when I made an impromptu lunch stop here a few weeks ago. The restaurant has a history of 60 years, serving authentic Karnataka-style non-vegetarian cuisine.  The reviewer tries a variety of dishes, praising the Mutton Keema, Mutton Dry, and Mutton Biryani. He highly recommends the Mutton Keema, describing it as a must-try. He also notes the quick service and the family-friendly atmosphere.  The highlight of the restaurant is its legacy, being run by three generations and serving homely food with a focus on flavour and quality, making it a must-visit for those seeking an authentic taste of Karnataka.

An eatery that began the Kamat Yatriniwas group’s foray into highway restaurants twenty seven years ago, Kamat Lokaruchi in Ramanagara serves the nourishing fare of rural Karnataka in an earthy atmosphere that seeks to connect diners to the land. Traditional staples are cooked over old fashioned stoves fuelled by wood to recreate authentic flavours of yore, the culinary philosophy employed here also shuns the use of artificial color and additives. Since they first opened doors, numerous eateries have mushroomed on the Mysuru highway, but even today, over quarter of a century later, Kamat Lokaruchi reigns supreme as one of the most popular eateries on the route. I caught up with Narayan Kamat, son of the late A. S. Kamat who established the Kamat Yatriniwas group, and also explored the kitchens and some wholesome dishes here. During my lunch visit a few months ago to Subbanna Mess, a 100-year-old eatery in the temple town of Melukote in Karnataka, I happened to steal a glance at the preparation of the thatte idli batter, for breakfast the next morning. I was intrigued by the high proportion of urad dal as compared to typical idlis, and so made a mental note to return. And when we did, we were rewarded with tasting one of the softest idlis that I have ever eaten, in combination with a delicious, warming  cucumber gojju made. I also savoured their scrumptious no-onion masala dosae, again with an interesting twist, and their world-famous creations - puliyogare, bella pongal and sakkare pongal. This is a breakfast that I will gladly return to, and I hope this video makes your day too. Take care, stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

100 year old vegetarian eatery in melukote, temple town, mandya district, pandavapura taluk, iyengar food, iyengar cuisine, brahmin cuisine, puliyogare, sakkarai pongal, bela pongal, sambar, rasam, banana leaf lunch, traditional meal, karnataka

Located around 150 kilometres from Bengaluru, the temple town of Melukote is home to culinary traditions that have evolved over centuries. Many say that quintessential Iyengar delicacies such as the sakkarai pongal, bela pongal and puliyogare trace their roots to this sacred town where one modest eatery, Subbanna Mess, has been serving traditional Melukote cuisine for nearly a century to pilgrims who journey here. In this episode, I explore the making of the puliyogare gojju, savour a delicious lunch and meet the family behind this eatery who state rather humbly, that they are merely preserving the culinary customs handed down by the generations that came before them.

Hope you enjoy this watch. Stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

During my lunch visit a few months ago to Subbanna Mess, a 100-year-old eatery in the temple town of Melukote in Karnataka, I happened to steal a glance at the preparation of the thatte idli batter, for breakfast the next morning. I was intrigued by the high proportion of urad dal as compared to typical idlis, and so made a mental note to return. Renowned for its traditional South Indian breakfast, the eatery offers a taste of history and authenticity. The star of the show is undoubtedly the incredibly soft Thatte Idli, a testament to the perfectly balanced rice-to-lentil ratio. Paired with their special gojju, a warm and flavorful cucumber-based gravy, it's a match made in food heaven. The Masala Dosa, too, boasts a unique twist with ginger and lime replacing onions, offering a refreshingly different flavor profile. The video highlights the Sakkarai Pongal and Bella Pongal, traditional sweet dishes that are sure to delight anyone with a sweet tooth. The highlight of Subbanna Mess is the unique taste and texture of their Thatte Idli, achieved by using a higher proportion of urad dal compared to typical idlis.

Located around 150 kilometres from Bengaluru, the temple town of Melukote is home to culinary traditions that have evolved over centuries. Many say that quintessential Iyengar delicacies such as the sakkarai pongal, bela pongal and puliyogare trace their roots to this sacred town where one modest eatery, Subbanna Mess, has been serving traditional Melukote cuisine for nearly a century to pilgrims who journey here. In this episode, I explore the making of the puliyogare gojju, savour a delicious lunch and meet the family behind this eatery who state rather humbly, that they are merely preserving the culinary customs handed down by the generations that came before them.

When offered a free stall at the Mysuru Dussehra exhibition 27 years ago, Zainul Ahbideen felt he should in turn offer the city a taste of something different. And for his main ingredient, he chose the humble gobi, cauliflower, given the popularity of gobi manchurian, but in an avatar that had not been seen before. Experimenting with a spice mix he first made at home, Usman Dry Gobi emerged. It wasn't long before he moved to a street cart, and eventually a streetside stall a few years ago. Great care is taken by him and his son, Usman, to procure the right quality and size of cauliflowers, that are cleaned thoroughly and spiced with a secret masala, before being fried meticulously in a bath of hot oil. The result is the crunchiest, most flavourful dry gobi one can eat in Mysuru, and the sheer number of customers who queue up at this stall every evening stand testament to the fact that Usman’s Dry Gobi has emerged as one of this palace city’s most popular street food creations over the years. https://goo.gl/maps/XkC4Ktg6mK2PouAU7.summary: This video features Usman Dry Gobi, a popular street food stall in Mysore, known for its crispy and flavorful dry gobi. The stall owner, Zainul Ahbideen, started this venture 27 years ago with the goal of offering something unique to the city. The star dish, dry gobi, is made with carefully selected cauliflowers, cleaned thoroughly, and fried to perfection with a secret spice mix.  The video highlights the dedication to quality, cleanliness, and the meticulous process that goes into creating this crunchy and delicious snack.  The host praises the texture, the balance of spices, and the overall taste of the dish, comparing the crunch to popcorn. He recommends eating it as is, without any chutney or lime, to savor its unique flavor. The popularity of the stall is evident from the long queue of eager customers.  Usman Dry Gobi is a testament to the simple yet satisfying nature of street food done right, making it a must-try when in Mysore.  The unique aspect is the dedication to quality and process, using the right cauliflower, cleaning it well, and frying it perfectly, resulting in a crunchy, flavorful gobi that has remained popular for 27 years.

The Savaji community, settled for centuries in Karnataka, traces its ancestry to a race of warriors, originally from Maharashtra, and therefore it only seems natural that meat, especially mutton, forms an important part of their diet. 

Hotel Savaji’s Bengaluru pays allegiance to its owner, Narasingsa Kathare’s Savaji culinary roots, when he got into this business 25 years ago owing to circumstances, unable to find a job despite possessing an engineering degree and mba. He began his eatery cooking all dishes himself, wIth recipes gleaned subconsciously having watched his grandmother cook in his ancestral home in Hubli. Therefore, not surprisingly,  the flavours are the sort that one would find in a Savaji household in North Karnataka, the food cooked in a set up that quite resembles a home kitchen, not by professional chefs, but a small team of people who moved from Hubli to join Narasingsa. I step in here for a delicious meal of a sumptuous, mutton thali with the softest kaima unde, tasty chicken masala, mutton dry fry and other dishes. If you like your meaty preparations, albeit spicy, this is certainly a place to check out Savaji cuisine in Bengaluru.

This tiny eatery isnt easy to locate, hidden on the first floor of a nondescript building in a bylane of Rajajinagar. But once you ve eaten here, the flavors are the sort that will be permanently ‘landmarked’ on your palate. 

Hope you enjoy this episode. Take care; stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

When in Arcot, Northeastern Tamil Nadu, those in the know make a beeline for Chettiyar Mittai Kadai, home of the legendary makkan peda that was first made here nearly two centuries ago by Govindasamy Chettiyar, inspired by a mithai that he tasted in the palace of the Nawab of Arcot. I caught up with his fifth generation, Mr. Sundaram, to find out what goes into the making of this flour and khoa dumpling stuffed with a mixture of 11 dry fruits and nuts, before being fried gently in oil over a wood fire until golden brown and then left to soak in sugar syrup. HR Ramaswamy Iyengar came to Bengaluru from Holenarsipur in 1956 and set up a bakery in Basavanagudi, an old market area surrounded by villages where groundnuts were cultivated. Selling a limited variety of pure vegetarian breads, buns and biscuits, the bakery fell upon hard times due to the rationing of flour and other essentials in the seventies. Faced with dire prospects, Ramaswamy Iyengar looked at the plentiful groundnut for survival and in doing so hit upon a unique recipe combining peanuts with a blend of spices that he named the Congress kadlekai, owing to the legend that during British times, secret notes were sent by Indian National Congress party workers hidden in sacks of groundnuts. I spent an afternoon with the second and third generation of the Sreenivasa Brahmins Bakery family to watch the making of the iconic Congress kadlekai and also taste some of the traditional items that make this 66-year-old institution a hit not just with locals, but also with Bengaluru diaspora across the globe who throng here for the kadlekai, nippat, khara buns, palya buns, puffs and other traditional Iyengar bakery treats.

Congress Kadlekai.summary: A unique and traditional Bengaluru snack made with peanuts, spices, and a hint of sugar. Its name comes from the pre-independence era when secret messages were transported in sacks of peanuts.

KBC (Khara Bun Congress).summary: A flavorful and buttery bun filled with a spiced potato mixture, Congress Kadlekai, and green chilies. A must-try for its unique combination of flavors and soft texture.

Palya Bun.summary: A delicious bun filled with a generous amount of flavorful potato palya.  The palya is made with smashed potatoes, onions, lentils, spices, and a hint of lime juice.

Capsicum Puff.summary: A crispy and flaky puff pastry filled with a flavorful and moist capsicum and onion mixture. The masala used in the filling is reminiscent of biryani spices, adding a unique twist.

Baked Nippat.summary: A healthier and crispier alternative to fried nippat, this baked version has a satisfying crunch and toasted notes. A great snack for those who prefer baked treats.

Honey Cake.summary: A traditional eggless honey cake that is heavy, sweet, and moist. It is generously coated with jam and desiccated coconut, making it a perfect treat for those with a sweet tooth.

HR Ramaswamy Iyengar came to Bengaluru from Holenarsipur in 1956 and set up a bakery in Basavanagudi, an old market area surrounded by villages where groundnuts were cultivated. Selling a limited variety of pure vegetarian breads, buns and biscuits, the bakery fell upon hard times due to the rationing of flour and other essentials in the seventies. Faced with dire prospects, Ramaswamy Iyengar looked at the plentiful groundnut for survival and in doing so hit upon a unique recipe combining peanuts with a blend of spices that he named the Congress kadlekai, owing to the legend that during British times, secret notes were sent by Indian National Congress party workers hidden in sacks of groundnuts. I spent an afternoon with the second and third generation of the Sreenivasa Brahmins Bakery family to watch the making of the iconic Congress kadlekai and also taste some of the traditional items that make this 66-year-old institution a hit not just with locals, but also with Bengaluru diaspora across the globe who throng here for the kadlekai, nippat, khara buns, palya buns, puffs and other traditional Iyengar bakery treats.

Congress Kadlekai.name: Congress Kadlekai
Congress Kadlekai.summary: A unique and iconic snack that originated in Bangalore. It features crunchy peanuts coated in a flavorful blend of spices, including turmeric, hing, chili powder, and curry leaves. The peanuts are split, adding to their distinctive texture. This snack has a fascinating history, as it is believed to be named after the Indian National Congress party, who used sacks of peanuts to transport secret messages during the British era.

KBC.name: KBC (Khara Bun Congress)
KBC.summary: A delicious combination of a Khara Bun (a savory bun) filled with Congress Kadlekai, butter, and spices. The bun is soft and flavorful, while the peanut filling adds a satisfying crunch and a burst of spice.

Palya Bun.name: Palya Bun
Palya Bun.summary: A hearty and flavorful bun filled with a generous portion of potato palya. The palya is a flavorful mixture of potatoes, onions, spices, and herbs. The bun is soft and complements the savory filling perfectly.

Capsicum Puff.name: Capsicum Puff
Capsicum Puff.summary: A flaky and savory puff pastry filled with a spicy and flavorful capsicum mixture. The capsicum filling is well-seasoned and has a satisfying crunch. This puff is perfect for those who enjoy a bit of heat.

Baked Nippat.name: Baked Nippat
Baked Nippat.summary: A healthier take on the classic Nippat, a crispy and savory snack. This version is baked instead of fried, giving it a satisfying crunch without the added oil. It is seasoned with spices and has a slightly sweet and nutty flavor.

Sreenivasa Brahmins Bakery, with its commitment to quality and flavor, has secured its place as a beloved institution in Bangalore's culinary landscape.

In our continuing initiative to support small businesses, we visit Momo Shop, a passion enterprise of Ronald George who fell in love with momos whilst pursuing an advanced mountaineering course in Darjeeling, with plans to eventually join the army like his father and brother, both war heroes. Unfortunately, that wasn’t to be owing to an accident, necessitating him to switch tracks to a corporate career. However, after 11 years, he decided to return to his love for momos in 2010 and set up a tiny 100 sq. ft. shop in RT Nagar, North Bengaluru to serve the freshest momos. How fresh? Unlike typical momo shops which pre-cook and reheat momos to serve customers instantly, out here these steamed dumplings are prepared from scratch, from rolling out the dough to preparing the filling, only when an order is placed. This approach has won for Ronald a steady stream of customers over the years, facilitating his shop’s move to a slightly larger space. Hope you enjoy this episode enough to support neighbourhood eateries like the Momo Shop. Take care; stay safe and strong.

Whilst many eateries are forced to cut back owing to the current situation, Bengaluru’s much-loved idli-chutney destination, Veena Stores, that began as a small condiment shop 44 years ago, has done just the opposite! It has scaled up four times in size! just so it can afford its customers more space and some relative peace of mind, valued aspects in present times, when tucking into their favourite tiffin treats here. Gone are the days when one had to struggle to order and then huddle and eat on the footpath. Instead, the store is now transformed with a dedicated ordering counter, a larger food dispensing area, indoor space, and even a traditional katte (alfresco bench) where one can sip on some coffee and take in the Malleswaram vibe. I caught up with second generation owner, Pradeep Suryanarayan, and also savoured a plate of idli vade and a couple of their other popular items. Hope you enjoy this episode; take care and stay safe. #idlvada #tiffin #vegetarian 

sri lakshmi venkateshwara coffee bar, slv, slv coffee bar, slv idli vada, south bangalore’s popular breakfast and tiffin destination, most popular idli and vada, vegetarian, khara bath, kesari bath, tiffin, banashankari bangalore, bengaluru

When it comes to savouring soft idlis and crunchy vadas, all roads in South Bengaluru lead to Sri Lakshmi Venkateshwara Coffee Bar, or SLV as this string of eateries is popularly known. And it is no surprise given the fact that the brothers behind this tiffin house enterprise have over 125 years of combined experience in the making of the idli, vada and khara bath, beginning with extended stints at the iconic Brahmins’ Coffee Bar where they learnt the trade. I met the brothers behind SLV, Srinivas Bhat, Krishna Bhat and Anantha Bhat at their flagship eatery as it completed 35 years last month to find out what makes their offerings so special.

Idli 
The idli is porous and the sort that dissolves in the mouth when steaming hot. The chutney makes for a flavourful accompaniment to permeate through the idli with its ‘flowing’ consistency and spicy fervour. One of the best idlis one can taste in Bengaluru. The butter, to be honest, is an unnecessary but decadently tasty indulgence!
Rs. 28 (usd 0.4) for two idlis; Rs. 10 (usd 0.1) for butter per idli 
10/10

Vada 
The vade here is double fried ensuring a crisp crunchy bite from the first bite to the last, on the inside it is soft and porous, speckled with black pepper, green chillies and curry leaves. 
Rs. 22 (usd 0.3) per vada
9/10

Chowchow Bath 
The khara bath is ‘runny’ in its texture and quite loaded in its flavour, one can taste the aroma of the spice mix that goes into the preparation here. The kesari bath is lush with ghee, and studded with pineapple flecks and cashew.
Rs. 46 (usd 0.6)
8.5/10

Coffee
Rs. 10 (usd 0.1)
8/10

https://goo.gl/maps/NH1dg3CQy6DiTKZX9.description:
#idlichutney #vadasambar #bangalore

popular neighbourhood eatery, south indian snacks, vegetarian, tiffin room, j p nagar, idli, vade, vada, chutney, sambar, masala dose, dosa, chow chow baath, khaara baath, kesari baath, local eatery, breakfast

Every city has its favourite dishes, and iconic eateries that are famous for dishing these out. Bengaluru too has its tiffin rooms and thindi houses that are destinations unto themselves and occupy pride of place in every must-eat-at list. However, unknown to many there are equally worthy eateries that have been serving neighbourhoods quietly for decades. They don’t get celebrated beyond the communities they serve and are quite content with no accolades coming their way. In this episode, I visit one such establishment, SN Refreshments, which has been a cornerstone of JP Nagar, South Bengaluru for its limited but much sought after refreshment fare for 30 years. Hope you enjoy this episode, take care and stay safe.

Happy Eating,
Kripal Amanna
Gourmet On The Road,
Food Lovers TV

Idli
The idli is soft, porous and grainy in its texture thanks to the proportion of idli rice and urad dal in the batter, and some rice rava. When dunked into the chutney, the idli readily absorbs much of it, almost falling apart in the process. The chutney is unique, the spicy note of green chilli is accentuated by some jaggery, before submitting to the fresh crunch of the coconut, the bite of the roasted gram and the flavours of the mustard seed-curry leaf oggarane (seasoning). A tasty sambar served alongside is almost glossed over not for any fault of its doing, but because the idli-chutney combination are superstars on their own. When here, enjoy the idli, ladled over with plenty of chutney.  
Rs. 15 per idli
9/10
10/10 (for the chutney)

Vade
The texture of the vade is textbook, crisp to the touch with a lacey crunch on the exterior, yielding and porous on the inside speckled with some green chilli, coriander and curry leaves. fried onions and minimal spicing. Crunchy on its own from the first bite to the last, the vade finds its soulmate in the chutney, its airy texture submitting to the embrace of the condiment. And if  you like a vada dip, the wholesome lentil sambar is happy to acquiesce with its sweet acidity of tomatoes and a whiff of asafoetida.
Rs. 20 per vade
9.5/10

Masala Dosa 
The masala dose is roasted to a golden brown with brownish striations. On the palate, it is crisp with a hint of tartness, and pleasing in its flavours minus the decadence of ghee and butter. The potato palya is creamy with the rich, savoury punch of onions. The chutney, though served in a ‘ghatti’ (solid consistency), is just as impactful as its runny avatar served with the idli and vade. 
Rs. 45/-
8/10

Chow Chow Baath 
The khaara baath and kesari baath are cooked to a texture that is near ‘runny’. The veggies in the khaara baath change each day, this time around, it was the capsicum and one could taste its vegetal notes and the fried onions, alongside the toasty notes of the curry leaves and the sour twang of a drizzle of lemon. The kesari baath is pleasing and the sort that passes muster with the taste buds, making for a sweet end to a thindi experience at SN refreshments. 
Rs. 46
8/10

Coffee
Rs. 12
7.5/10

https://goo.gl/maps/jP638xbjdGBY55EUA.description:
#VegetarianBreakfast #AuthenticBreakfast #GourmetOnTheRoad

SSP Refreshments, also known as Mudanna Hotel, Mixing Hotel, Jayanagar, Bangalore, serves rare Bangalore Idli, Acrey Idli, Acre idli, Ikrey Idli, Pulav, Vegetable Pulav, Palav, Chitranna, Vada, Uppitu, Mosaru Anna, Vegetarian Breakfast, Bangalore, Breakfast, Idli, Chutney, Mudanna Pulav

With recipes gleaned from his father-in-law, Devaraju and his wife began a small venture out of their home nearly 30 years ago, serving what is now a rare Bangalore breakfast delicacy, the Acrey Idli. Since then, SSP Refreshment House has amassed a formidable reputation for its limited menu, an aromatic vegetable pulav, chitranna and a couple of other dishes, that run out not too long from the time they open doors to their home at 7 am.

Food Lovers’ editor, Kripal Amanna savours some of the dishes and also peeps into the kitchen to chat with the family and catch the making of the now-largely-lost Bengaluru Acrey Idli. Enjoy! 

Acrey Idli 
The idli is soft and unbelievably pliable, melts in the mouth when hot. You can smell the gentle sweet aroma of the batter which is perfectly fermented rendering a springy fluffiness to the idli. The thick, spicy lentil chutney with flecks of dry coconut makes for a great accompaniment.
Rs. 20 (usd 0.3)
9/10

Chitranna 30/ 20
You can taste the gentle tartness of the lemon, the flavour of cumin and pointed notes of green chilli on the palate, the lentils in the seasoning make for a nice bite.
Rs. 20/30 (usd 0.3/ 0.4) for half/ full portion
7/10

Pulav 
A flavourful pulav with the lingering warmth that comes from spices such as cinnamon and cloves, this is what draws customers to SSP. There’s the spicy kick of green chilli, but juxtaposed against the other ingredients, its hit is not the sort that obliterates your tastebuds. The seasoned chutney served alongside adds a layer of pleasing nuttiness. 
Rs. 20/30 (usd 0.3/0.4) for half/ full portion
8.5/10

Mosaru Anna  
Gentle on the palate, this provides cooling respite if one has overindulged in the spicy pulav and chutney.
Rs. 20/30 (usd 0.3/ 0.4) for half/ full portion
7.5/10

taaza thindi, must-visit for its tasty south indian tiffin, hygienically prepared and affordable! vegetarian, breakfast, tiffin, south canara cuisine, taaza thindi, jayanagar, bengaluru, bangalore, lunch, popular eatery, south indian, karnataka, masala dose, masala dosa, idli, vada, chow chow baath, khaara baath, kesari baath, coffee

When it comes to the hygiene aspect in a mainstream eatery, Taaza Thindi rivals the best with its clean approach to cooking and serving delicious South Indian tiffin fare. Not due to current covid 19 compulsions, but from when they began operations six years ago. In the current scenario, they have taken matters a step further as I discovered when I visited their flagship Jayanagar restaurant recently to savour their best selling masala dose. Turns out they have stopped making dosas altogether just because the three to four-minute ensuing wait for one would have customers crowding, making it difficult to maintain social distancing owing to space issues at this outlet. “It’s a huge loss financially especially in these difficult times”, say the founders, but “we didn’t want to compromise with the wellbeing of our customers and employees!” 
Mildly disappointed with the absence of the dosa, I sought solace in their equally pleasing idli vada and chow chow baath combo, the latter featuring a comforting khaara baath made with bansi rawa. Hope you enjoy this episode, stay safe and happy eating.

tks iyengar, bengaluru, bangalore, iyengar cuisine, lunch, vegetarian lunch, soppina saaru, akki rotti, payasa, popular lunch, south indian lunch, basaveshwar nagar

TKS Iyengar’s, a passion enterprise spanning three generations of a family came as a breath of fresh air to Bengaluru's tiffin culture with time honoured recipes that were hitherto confined to homes. Not surprisingly, this charming refreshment house became an instant hit when they opened doors a year ago. However, the current covid situation has brought all that to nought, and left the family with no staff and barely any business to make ends meet. However, rather than buckle down, the ladies of the house aided by their menfolk are doing all that it takes to keep their traditions alive, from manning the stoves to serving customers to keeping house. I savour a delicious homestyle Iyengar meal on a recent visit, and while doing so said a silent prayer, hoping that eateries like TKS Iyengar’s survive these turbulent times. For if not, we would be much poorer in losing the rich, ancient culinary traditions of our land. Take care and stay safe.

Previous TKS Iyengar’s Video link:

Meals

And to end your meal, a payasam for the day. All this for Rs. 100 only!
Rs. 100 (usd 1.3) 
8/10

https://goo.gl/maps/n6zmWZre9cHaMB9a9.title: IYENGAR HOMESTYLE Breakfast At TKS IYENGAR’s |UNIQUE DISHES! Nuchinna Unde, BaleEle Idli, Hayagreeva
https://goo.gl/maps/n6zmWZre9cHaMB9a9.description:
#VegetarianBreakfast #AuthenticBreakfast #GourmetOnTheRoad

TKS Iyengar’s must-visit for authentic Iyengar dishes. Three Generations Family Recipes, Vegetarian, No Garlic, Unique Homestyle Dishes, bale elle idli, thatte idli, classic idli, nuchinna unde, puliyogare, ottu shavige, god halubai, hayagreeva, sweet pongal, bangalore, breakfast

This recent entrant to Bengaluru’s vegetarian dining landscape located in the suburb of Basaveshwaranagar serves up Iyengar homestyle fare. Food Lovers’ Editor, Kripal Amanna visits this eatery for a late breakfast where he tastes an array of dishes, some hitherto unseen in restaurants, such as the Nuchinna Unde, Halubai, Hayagreeva (originally prepared as a temple offering), Ottu Shavige and more. He also meets the three generations of the TKS Iyengar family that is seeking to share its interesting culinary traditions with the people of Bengaluru though this endearing enterprise. Enjoy!

Bale Elle Idli 
The Bale Elle Idli carries with it the subtle aroma of the banana leaf in which it is steamed. The leaf also imbues the idli with a light colouring. You bite into the crunch of coconut and the lentils as you taste the idli, savour it with the sambar that’s perfect in its sour-sweet balance and the spirited chutney. Rs. 30 (usd 0.4) for 2 pcs
9/10

Thatte Idli
A deliciously delicate thatte idli, springy like it should be. Acts as the perfect canvas of sorts to soak up the flavours of the chutney and sambar.
Rs. 30 (usd 0.4) for 2 pcs
8.5/10

Classic Idli
Grainy in texture and porous, but pales in comparison to the bale elle and thatte idli served here.
Rs. 12 (usd 0.2)
7/10

Nuchinna Unde
If you need only one reason to visit TKS Iyengar, these steamed dumplings made of four lentil varieties would be it. A traditional Iyengar recipe wouldn’t use onions, but these are added here due to the wants of running a commercial establishment, which lends it a delightful crunch alongside the lentils. Rs. 30 (usd 0.4) for 2 pcs
10/10

Puliyogare
Cooked and cooled rice, flavoured with spicy tamarind paste and fortified with the crunch of lentils and ground lentils, this is a Iyengar classic with the perfect balance of flavours - touch of sweet that gives into sour and the warmth of  the spices. The puliyogare here is made with red rajamudi rice from Hassan. 
Rs. 50 (usd 0.7)
9/10

Ottu Shavige
This sweet and ‘khaara’ combo is served with ella pudi (a powder made of sesame seeds, peanuts and jaggery) gasgase (poppy seed) payasa and a nutty, spicy chutney, enlivened with mustard oil and red chillies.  
Rs. 60 (usd 0.8)
9/10

Godhi Halubai
Made with puree of wheat, coconut milk and jaggery, this wobbly pudding like dessert magically disappears into sweet ‘nothingness’ when you place a piece in your mouth.
Rs. 10 (usd 0.15)
8/10

Hayagreeva 
Taste the creaminess of lentils and the bite of dried coconut and cashew nuts in this decadently sweet dessert that was originally made as an offering to Lord Hayagreeva. 
Rs. 50 (usd 0.7)
8.5/10

Sweet Pongal
The whiff of edible camphor that greets you on the palate disappears quickly into the background, leaving you to relish the milky richness of this rice and lentil dessert.
Rs. 50 (usd 0.7)
8/10

Coffee 
Nice way to end things after an indulgent meal here.
Rs. 10 (usd 0.15)
7/10

#Idli #Breakfast #GourmetOnTheRoad

This tiny shop in Malleshwaram is popular for their fluffy idlis and crunchy vadas. Originally a condiment store in 1977, Veena stores has amassed a loyal customer base over three decades of service. 

Food Lovers’ Editor Kripal Amanna finds people of all ages, crowding around the tiny store to savour a delicious breakfast from Veena Stores. He samples some of the more popular items on the menu such as the Idli Vada, the Chow Chow Bath and a unique Sweet Pongal. 

GOURMET ON THE ROAD RATING
IDLI 
the idlis have an inviting fragrance. soft but with just enough texture. the chutney packs a punch with coriander, chilli, and curry leaves. exactly what you need with the soft idlis.  
9/10
Rs 45

VADA
vada is crisp, and crunchy, with a porous inside. very mildly seasoned with tiny flecks of coconut. definitely needs the chutney for that flavour boost.
8/10

KHARA BATH 
soft, creamy, and flavourful, even without the onions and garlic. this khara bath packs all the flavour of the tomatoes, curry leaves, and chillies. its taste lingers on your palate. 
8.5/10

KESARI BATH
the kesari bath itself is not too sweet. the plump raisin gives it a burst of sweetness and the cashews add a toasty flavour!
8/10

7/10

JAGGERY PONGAL
The jaggery is very evident in this short-grained rice dish, as is the edible camphor that immediately engulfs the palate. A touch of lentils add some creamy graininess to the bite.
8.5/10

COFFEE
the coffee is nice, thick, and strong. always the best end to a tiffin breakfast. 
Rs. 
7/10

This pillar in Bengaluru’s culinary landscape has always had only four items on its menu! For 5 decades Brahmin’s Coffee Bar has been serving up the softest idlis, crunchy vadas, and of course, thick, strong coffee in South Bengaluru. 

In this episode of Gourmet On The Road, Food Lovers’ Editor Kripal Amanna visits the famous coffee bar and samples everything on the menu (all four items that is), which consists of the Idli Vada, the Khara Bath, and the Kesari Bath. Idli and Vada 
the idli is unbelievably soft, pillowy, and melts in your mouth with no effort! this is in contrast to the perfect crunch of the vada. the inside of the vada is almost cloud-like, speckled with slivers of coconut, chillies, and curry leaves. the chutney is spicy and slightly minty. this dish, especially the idli is a revelation! 
Rs 16 for one Idli

Rs 23.
9/10

a coffee, nice, strong and thick coffee. just the way it should be!
Rs 16.

https://goo.gl/maps/qR9ALXXmRBrGSbYe6.description:
#Bangalore #IdliDosa #GourmetOnTheRoad

Dose Manjanna, Must Try Salem Idli, Butter Idli, Onion Open Dosa, Mysore Masala Dosa, Jayanagar, Bengaluru, Vegetarian, Street Food


Manjanna ran a popular street cart for 48 years in the South Bengaluru suburb of Jayanagar selling only three or four dishes, dose, idli and vada, earning him the moniker, Dose Manjanna. His son, Ganesh, seeks to keep alive his late father’s legacy in a tiny shop, aptly named Dose Manjanna, serving a smattering of traditional and some accidentally inspired creations, like the buttery, spicy Salem Idli. Concocted on a cold, rainy night, when his store had run out of hot idlis, in a bid to acquiesce to a customer’s demand for hot food just prior to the latter’s boarding a bus for Salem. 

In this #gourmetontheroad episode, Food Lovers’ editor, Kripal Amanna tastes the Salem Idli, a scrumptious ghee onion dose and a couple of other tiffin treats that has Jayanagar’s denizens crowding this eatery at all times. Hope you enjoy this episode.

SALEM IDLI
This Idli roasted in butter, sings the flavour of the butter with the spicy, grainy crunch of the podi. Eat it piping hot, just off the tawa. When it cools down, pair it with the spicy hurigadale (fried gram) chutney.
Rs. 20 (usd 0.3)
8.5/10

Butter Idli 
Thatte idli roasted on a hot tawa over melted butter, with lashings of butter and served with a dollop of butter, this is sheer decadence. The idli loses some its fervour as it begins to cool, and that’s when you taste its slight tartness.
Rs. 20 (usd 0.3)
8/10

Open Onion Dose
Served folded, this crisp, kadak dose was the highlight for me. Dripping with ghee and butter, smeared with chutney podi, a generous sprinkling of moist, crunchy onions, this dose is flavourful enough to be eaten on its own. The chutneys served alongside play a distant second fiddle to this open onion dose. 
Rs. 40 (usd 0.6)
9/10

Mysore Masale Dose
The masale is smeared into a paste with chutney podi, butter and onions as the dose is roasted on the tava. I expected it to be robust in its flavours, however the potatoes seem to tone down the aggression of the chutney podi, making this a gently-spiced bite. Mix together the gram chutney, chutney podi and butter that’s served alongside, and combine with the dose to savour a spicy mouthful. 
Rs. 40 (usd 0.6)
8/10

Shavige Baath 
The shavige baath here is light, fluffy and springy, tossed in a chitranna or lemon rice masala. Studded liberally with peanuts, fried lentils, flecks of green chilli and roasted curry leaves, it makes a gentle yet persuasive impression on the palate. If you like it spicy, enjoy it with the smokey tomato-red chilli-roasted gram chutney.
Rs. 30 (usd 0.4)
8.5

https://goo.gl/maps/eyJ7E26hKvmKhqji6.description:
#shineshetty #actor #foodtruck 

popular food truck run by kannada actor shine shetty, big boss kannada winner, inspirational story, vegetarian, mangalorean food, sabakki idli, mysore masala dosa, dose, bela kai neer dose, galli kitchen, banashankari, south bengaluru, bangalore

During a particularly difficult period in his career, popular Kannada actor, Shine Shetty took up cooking to stretch his meagre resources and feed himself. Cooking in those difficult times led him to mull the idea of setting up a food truck venture for his livelihood. Rustling up a loan from well wishers, he found a second auto that he could afford. Thus began Galli Kitchen, a streetside food enterprise, a far cry from the world of glitz and glamour that Shetty was once used to. Two years on though, Galli Kitchen seems to have changed the fortunes of its owner, and has now upgraded to a full-sized food truck. I catch up with this affable actor over an inspiring chat, and also taste some of the popular fare here.

Sabakki Idli
An idli that isn't too thick to hold, but weighty nonetheless owing to the sabudana or tapioca pearls. The aroma of the dill takes over the palate when placed in the mouth, the texture is a bit gummy. The idli is the sort that comes alive when combined with the chutneys, especially the spicy and sour notes of the kempu chutney. 
Rs. 40 (usd 0.6)
8.5/10
9/10 for the kempu chutney

Mysore Masala Dose
Shine Shetty’s ode to the 99-variety style of dose that would sustain him during his acting school days in Mumbai. The dose is crisp when it leaves the tava, but weighed down to a soft texture by the loaded stuffing of masala, fresh onions and tomatoes, when gathered into a tight roll. The spicy-sweet flavour of the podi is discernible above the fresh crunch of the veggies. Not a dose for the purist, but a tasty and filling one nonetheless.
Rs. 50 (usd 0.7)
8/10

Neer Dosa Bela Kai
This is how Mangaloreans love to eat their neer dose for breakfast with a lip smacking accompaniment of fresh coconut, jaggery and ghee combined together with a touch of cardamom. Simple yet delicious, and a must order to finish your thindi experience on a sweet note at Galli Kitchen.
Rs. 40 (0.6)
9/10

Happy Eating!

Kripal Amanna,
Gourmet On The Road,
Food Lovers TV

iyer idly, east bengaluru’s most popular idli shop, popular bangalore breakfast, idli chutney, healthy breakfast

Iyer Idly, a tiny shop opened 19 years ago, selling idli batter to a community of busy scientists and engineers in the East Bengaluru neighbourhood of Vignan Nagar. In time, the shop added hot idlis in response to customer requests, and has since served only the idli and nothing else! The founder, Mr. M K Mahadevan passed on a few years ago, but his legacy continues with his wife, Mrs. Uma Devan and son, Krishnan Mahadevan, who till date make idlis the old-fashioned way, each batch of rice and urad dal batter fermented overnight, before being steamed and served with a spicy chutney that has won numerous fans for Iyer Idly not just in its neighbourhood but across the city. Fans who savour nearly 50,000 of these hot, fluffy idlis each month. Hope you enjoy this episode. Take care and stay safe.

Idli Chutney 
The idlis are made the traditional way from idli rice and urad dal that is ground to a batter and fermented overnight. The result is an idli that is soft and grainy, slightly pasty and aromatic, with a touch of tartness. It is served with a spicy chutney that some say is more popular than the idli here. This combination though is definitely the sort that makes Iyer Idly a sought after destination for what is perhaps one of Bengaluru’s favourite breakfast dishes. 
Rs 10 (usd ) per idli
9/10

A tiny village located atop the Charmadi ghat in Mudigere taluk of Karnataka, Kottigehara was a mere bus stop on this old route to Dakshina Kannada. Travellers would stop here for a few minutes and if hungry, would saunter off to one of the few home eateries on this remote, narrow strip of highway. And perhaps because its quick batter, water-like in its consistency, required almost no prep when an unexpected guest walked in, the neer dosae (neer meaning ‘water’ in kannada) quickly became the staple offering of this village centered around a bus stand. Whist many neer dosa stalls have mushroomed since, the oldest home eatery here is Anil Hotel, begun by Mrs. Mary 48 years ago and now managed by her son, Baby and his wife, Theresia. Famous for its honestly-priced homestyle curries, tasty preparations and warming hospitality that I first experienced a year ago, I learnt that the eatery was recently rebuilt after being demolished in highway expansion causing untold challenges to the family. In this episode, we revisit this tiny enterprise to not just savour their fare for the day but to also support them as they make a new beginning despite having a legacy of nearly half a century. 

Hope you enjoy this episode. Take care; stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

In her tiny eatery, just off the highway in Sakleshpur, Mrs. Vishalakshi Lokesh cooks homestyle non vegetarian fare - biryani, khaima unde, mutton chops, chilli chicken, etc. - to recipes she learnt decades ago from her mother in Bengaluru, but accommodating ingredients more suited to native Malenadu tastes. The result is comforting, tasty food that not only has its share of customers amongst the local populace, but also draws in travellers on the route. This enterprise that she began with her late husband, Mr. Lokesh, 21 years ago, supported by son Sujith today, may seem a bit rustic in its aesthetics, but more than makes up for it in the honest, homely appeal of a meal here. Say the word, ‘Pabba’s’ to anyone in Mangalore, or someone who has had the opportunity to visit this port city, and one is most likely to be met with a smile or in the very least, warming thoughts of  wistfulness. For very few, if at all any, in Kudla may have escaped to the alluring charm of the gadbad, tiramisu, parfait, bella candy and scores of other delicious ice cream creations concocted by S. Prabhakar Kamath, affectionately known as Pabba to family and friends, over half a century at his now iconic Mangalorean institution, Pabba’s and Ideal Ice Creams. On my visit to kudla nearly a couple of months ago, I had the opportunity to sit with him (after nearly 20 years), his son, Mukund, and grandson, Mohith, to taste their latest creation, the I. Thali, a tantalising ice cream take on the South Indian thali, at their newest parlour, Pabba’s Ideal Café, Bharath Mall, that seems to have taken Mangalore by storm going by the sheer numbers that queue outside this large restaurant. However little did I know then, that this would be my last meeting with him! This episode was conceived as a review of the I Thali, but is now in some ways a tribute to the man who put Mangalore and his legendary ice creams on the culinary map.

South Canara has its share of seafood eateries, but then, there are some that have endeared themselves to diners over decades by virtue of being true to the traditions they follow. One such popular seafood stop is Hotel Mahalaxmi, in the fishing village of Malpe, about six kilometres from Udupi, where Mrs. Pushpavati Bangera, the matriarch of this family run restaurant that began as a tiny hut, has been cleaning the fish and preparing the masala for the fish curry and fry each day for the last 60 years. I catch up with her and her son, Vishwanath Bangera before I sit down to a satisfying fish thali meal.

K. N. Vasudeva Adiga’s Paakashala chain of restaurants may be relatively new, but those in the know speak volumes of his and his family’s culinary legacy that spans decades. Native to Africa and Middle East, and imported first into the country decades ago as part of a food security programme, the tilapia, a rather productive species of fish, came to be known as jilapia in native tongues, eventually acquiring the moniker ‘jilebi’ meenu or fish. And the tiny village of Buyyanadoddi in Mandya district, 90 kilometres outside Bengaluru, is making ripples with food lovers for its “jilebi” fish fry. 

The fish is caught fresh from streams in the area, marinated and then tawa fried over a wood fire, slathered continuously with a spicy green chilli paste and liberal sprinklings of crushed pepper, in a clutch of home eateries here. And over the years, its appeal seems to be catching on not just with locals but also Bangaloreans looking for a tasty outing and to experience Buyyanadoddi’s rustic appeal.

at Istta cafe, in terms of the aim and vision that they have for this enterprise. And of
course, there’s a whole bunch of food too. I think let’s taste some of the must haves
here at Istta cafe. So, do you guys come here regularly?

I certainly must say, they have a fairly large menu. So, you have got a bunch of chaats,
some sandwiches, some burgers, quick bites, like twisters, smilies, about six or seven
shakes, ice creams, hot beverages, sundaes, ice cream sizzlers as well, tender coconut
jelly and some juices. And what I am told is that, in the juices,
they make the juices with the tender coconut water, there’s no water (normal), but the
tender coconut water, that they combine with the juices. So, let us do one Istta special, tender coconut
jelly with the mango, we’ll do one aloo lachcha tokri, we’ll do one palak chaat,
since everybody is recommending it, we’ll also do one kheer ice cream. We have just ordered two or three things that
we were told are on Istta must haves. And that Istta must have is interesting, because
these are dishes that the cafe has experimented with over the last couple of months, and these
are dishes that the customers seem to be returning for. So, this is the aloo lachcha tokri, I’m
scared of approaching this. I think, while that lachcha tokri was made and kept, I was
waiting for my spinach chaat to be prepared. So, therefore, this has become a little soft.

 ompudi  or the sev that’s sprinkled on top, from the spicy khaara boondi, and that potato,
albeit fried, makes for a nice starchy medium to cradle the voluminous stuffing that goes
into this aloo lachcha tokri. There’s some papdi here. I think if you
have one of these aloo lachcha tokris here, you pretty much don’t need anything else.
I like the flavour of the papdi as well, there’s a certain butteriness to that papdi and also
I can taste some ajwain in that somewhere. I think that chaat is all about balance. You
need to find some sort of balance, some sort of harmony between all the ingredients that
go into the chaat. So, out here, you’re tasting a bit of that warmth from that green
chutney, but then you have that sweetness that comes from that sweet chutney. There’s also some tamarind in there, so
that brings in a bit of sourness, a bit of acidity. And then the creamines of the sweet dahi, of the yoghurt, seems to cradle it all. I think I should taste that palak chaat while
it is still crispy. So, this is basically made sev puri style, but instead of having
the puri at the bottom, you have spinach, spinach that’s dipped in a batter, in a
chickpea flour batter, with some red chilli powder, with some salt, some ajwain, jeera
etc., and then topped with an assemblage that’s quite similar to what would go on top of a
sev puri. After that dahi-laden aloo tokri chaat, this
feels a bit dry, but what’s nice is the weight of the spinach, of the spinach papadi. That spinach makes for a delicious twist to
that papdi that would otherwise typically be cradling a sev puri. So, in this spinach papdi chaat, you had two
options, one was to get it with some dahi and the other one was to get it more dry,
like the sev puri, because I got the lachcha aloo tokri with the dahi, I said let’s do
this the sev puri style, a bit dry. But I think that dahi would have certainly
helped bring all the disparate components together. Between the two, my vote goes to that aloo
lachcha tokri. So, what you have is a basket made of grated potato that’s wrapped around a mould, shaped and then deep fried in oil. And that basket, makes for a delicious fried
potato starchy base to accommodate the dozens of components that go into the making of this lachcha aloo tokri. If you find yourself here, this is certainly
something to order. Tender coconut jelly with mango. Kheer ice cream, just one, and one of the
biryani, veg biryani, one one. That looks like a loaded dessert. One more… thank you. Well, looks like I’m going to make a meal
of my desserts here at Istta cafe. Oh! Well, after those chaats, we’re onto our
desserts here at Istta cafe, and this is again from the ‘must have here’ list. This is
a coconut, a tender coconut mango jelly, and this is topped with some coconut cream and all sorts of dry fruit goodness. This, I am told, is also a vegan dessert, so if you want
vegan desserts, well, that tender coconut special, that Istta special with the mango,
they also have an option, a variation with the jackfruit, that’s something that you
must try. And then you have a couple of ice creams that have been made specifically for them, this is a very popular kheer ice cream, and then
I am told this ice cream is more or less a work in progress. And this flavour is called
the veg biryani. I heard the word veg biryani and I had to order it. They warned me though that this veg biryani ice cream isn’t where they would like it to be, but I said I must taste it. But, let’s
make a beginning, with that tender coconut mango jelly. When I looked at this assemblage, I thought
this would be a heavy dessert, but then you realize that most of the volume is made by
that tender coconut mango jelly. Although it has volume, it doesn’t have weight and
the resultant heaviness. And that coconut milk too is rather light.
This isn’t the thick coconut milk, but a slightly runnier coconut milk and I think
because it’s in combination with that jelly, that jelly is quite watery, so it tends to
dilute that coconut milk a little further. And then you’re tasting the crunch of the
nuts. I can taste some of the shaved almonds, some of the cashew that’s gone into it and
also, some figs that have been sprinkled on top of this dessert. That definitely is an interesting dessert
for you to savour, when you’re here at Istta cafe. And I must also complement the team here,
that despite all the challenges that they’re working with; they’re only about two months
old, and this is not a mere cafe, but an enterprise that hopes to be a movement that will empower
those with special abilities. For the kind of work that they have set out
to do, I must commend them on most of the things that I have tasted thus far. That lachcha aloo tokri is certainly something, is certainly a chaat that I would recommend, as also this tender coconut mango jelly, topped with some mango flavoured coconut milk. And because they use the pulp when they’re
making that jelly, and also perhaps that goes into that coconut cream, that coconut milk,
you can taste that sweetness of the mango and also that slightly sour twang. I think, let's move on next, to the ice creams.
This is the kheer ice cream… mmmm! . From a vegan dessert to one that is rich in
the flavour of the milk and the cream! Mmm! Plenty of dry fruits in there, so it’s almost
like a milk cream, a thick milk cream that has been frozen into an ice cream… You find plenty of nuts and raisins in every
spoon of that kheer ice cream. I think both these, the tender coconut mango jelly topped with the coconut cream and that kheer ice cream, have hit the spot Some water before I switch to that veg biryani ice cream… just to cleanse my palate. The texture of this ice cream (kheer) is creamy, but as I spoon this veg biryani ice cream, it certainly seems to be a lot more icy, more
sorbet-like in its texture. You can definitely taste some of the flavours of the whole spices that would go into tempering the ghee or the oil, in the beginning stages
of the biryani, so perhaps some cinnamon there, some cloves, some tej patta (bay leaf), perhaps some star anise too. They perhaps boil the milk in those spices and also the sugar, to
make this veg biryani ice cream. Flavour-wise, it’s a bit different, it’s
not something that you would typically associate with ice creams, but I think makes for an
interesting variation on one. But if you’re looking for something that’s
a little more traditional, comforting, an ice cream that you wouldn’t want to share,
I think that kheer ice cream, my tongue is frozen after all these desserts, certainly
is the one to try. Mmm! That’s a delicious ice cream. I love
the richness of the milk, of the cream, and the generous sprinkling of the dry fruits,
of the nuts, that you will find in every spoon of this ice cream. This is Rs. 50 for roughly about a couple
of scoops I think, well worth the price and so is that tender coconut mango jelly with
the coconut cream, that delicious vegan dessert. When I ventured out to Istta cafe this evening, I was looking to merely lend some support to what I think is a very interesting and
noble enterprise. This is an enterprise that seeks to empower those with special abilities. This is an enterprise that seeks to empower
them and make them independent. They made a beginning with this cafe, here
in Rajarajeshwari nagar, but they’re hoping this can grow as a movement that can support many people like Mohan and Vinayak to make something of their lives. And I think that's
the wonderful thing about this enterprise. Initiatives like these need to be supported,
because they allow these individuals, who otherwise face numerous hurdles and challenges, to integrate well into society, and also make something of themselves. Sure, you want to support an initiative that’s
doing great work, that has noble objectives, but you also wouldn’t mind some interesting tasty food along the way. And that lachcha tokri that I tasted, and also that tender
coconut mango jelly along with that kheer ice cream have certainly proved to be that. So, if you want to savour some interesting
cafe fare and also lend your support to a noble initiative along the way, definitely
check out ISTTA cafe here in Rajarajeshwari nagar. I hope you have enjoyed this very special
Gourmet On The Road episode. Until the next time, take care, stay safe and happy eating.

Tucked away in a nook of South Bengaluru, ISTTA cafe is the brainchild of IT professionals, Vasumathi Rajashekar and Prem Nithin R. This cafe hopes to evolve into a movement that will empower the lives of those with special abilities who struggle to integrate into society. The cafe offers a variety of tasty cafe fare, snacks, and desserts.  
What makes this cafe unique is that it is run by specially-abled individuals, providing them with an opportunity to be independent and showcase their skills.  The cafe is a testament to their dedication and hard work, with delicious food and a heartwarming purpose, making it a must-visit  spot.

Pandavapura, located on the state highway between Srirangapatna and Melukote in Mandya district of Karnataka, would perhaps not have registered as a breakfast stop on the traveller’s map, but for an idli shop that goes back over three decades. Actually, it isn’t even a shop, but a window in 60-something-year-old Shivappa’s home from where he dispenses freshly steamed idlis (only) with home churned butter for a few hours each morning. Travellers on the route, and even those who journey from afar just to eat here, line up outside the window, even before it is flung open at 7am.

Shivappa’s enterprise bears no signboard and he employs no one, preferring to do everything himself, from preparing the chutney and the butter to the soaking and grinding of the grain, the fermentation and steaming of the idlis, helped only by his wife. When you are here, you need to abide by his “seemingly authoritarian” rules - register your order, collect a token in exchange for your payment, and wait patiently for Shivappa to steam the idlis fresh and call your token number! This may seem like a bit of a drill, until you take a bite of the spicy chutney soaked idlis, and then it all seems to make sense. Like we discovered when we drove 130 kilometres from Bengaluru for breakfast recently. Hope you enjoy this episode; take care, stay safe and happy eating.

Invented as an unfussy double roti (bread) snack in the Kutch region of Gujarat over half a century ago, the dabeli (meaning pressed, in Gujarati) has since travelled the state and beyond, gaining popularity for its delicious composition - potatoes enlivened with a medley of spices, fruit, condiments, crunchy nuts and fritters, stuffed into a pav - that tingles with the sharpness of sweet, spicy and sour flavours. And like every other crowd-pleasing culinary creation, the dabeli too has spawned multiple avatars, this street cart that I visited had over 10, including a decadent double butter, cheese and dry fruit loaded version too. But it was the original, non-pretentious Kutchi Dabeli, resonating in its myriad flavours and textures, dished out by Yogesh Rathod at his Dabeliwala.com streetfood enterprise that made the most memorable impression on my palate. babusingh’s thakur pedha, famous dharwad pedha, original dharwad pedha, mithai, dharwad peda, dharwad, babusingh thakur pedha, hubli, hubbali, north karnataka food tour, dharwad food trail, dharwad food tour, hubli food trail, hubli food tour
 
There can be no mention made of Dharwad without its most renowned export, the Dharwad Pedha. Not many know this, but the original version made at Babusingh’s Thakur Dharwad Pedha has a legacy that goes back over 150 years when a halwai (sweetmeat cook), Ramratan Singh migrated to Karnataka from Unnao near Lucknow to escape the plague. A new beginning was made in Dharwad where he would roam the markets with a tray of unique pedha to sell. It was only a matter of time before the taste of this roasted khoya creation caught the fancy of local palates, and like they say, the rest is history. Generations later, the Dharwad Pedha may be shipped across the globe, but is still handmade the old-fashioned way. I met with Karan Singh, sixth generation of the Babusingh’s Thakur family to learn more about the making of this iconic Dharwad mithai. Hope you enjoy this episode. Take care, stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

belgaum’s most famous biryani, popular biryani restaurant in belgaum, niyaaz biryani belgaum, chicken biryani, mutton biryani, biryani making, belagavi, belgaum, belagavi biryani, niyaz belgaum biryani, niyaaz hotel belgaum biryani recipe, north karnataka food tour, belgaum food trail, belgaum food trail, belgaum food tour

How do biryanis become iconic? Well, most begin as tentative experiments and over a period of time endear themselves to the palate of the locals. So much so that the denizens of the place become vocal ambassadors for the biryani. And when it comes to Belagavi (Belgaum), the Niyaaz biryani is one such icon. Made in the kacchi akhni style, in which semi-cooked rice is layered over twice-marinated meat and cooked on dum, the Niyaaz biryani is subtle in its character, owing to a unique blend of spices, and the light fragrance of a short-grain locally grown rice that is used in combination with the more typical long grain basmati rice. What began as a family’s endeavour to create a unique biryani 30 years ago is now unarguably one of Belagavi’s most popular dishes. In this episode, I drive to Belgaum to meet co-owner, Niyaaz Abdussalam Saudagar, and explore in depth the making of both the chicken and mutton biryani, before proceeding to make a meal of these distinct Belagavi culinary signatures. Hope you enjoy this one; take care, stay safe and strong. Happy eating!

Chicken Biryani.summary: A subtle and aromatic biryani made with a blend of spices, tender chicken, and a combination of medium-grain Belagavi basmati and long-grain rice. The chicken is marinated twice and cooked to perfection, resulting in a moist and flavorful dish. The biryani is known for its balanced flavors and the use of fried onions (brista) that adds a slightly sweet tinge.

Mutton Biryani.summary: Similar in preparation to the chicken biryani, the mutton biryani features tender mutton cooked with the same aromatic blend of spices. The mutton, with its rich flavors and juices, infuses the rice, resulting in a wholesome and flavorful dish. The biryani is known for its soft and tender meat and a generous amount of masala that adds a delightful kick.

https://www.google.com/maps/place/Niyaaz.summary: This video takes viewers on a culinary journey to Niyaaz Restaurant in Belagavi, renowned for its iconic Belagavi biryani. The host delves into the history of the restaurant, learning how the family's legacy in spice trading has influenced their unique biryani recipe. Viewers are given an exclusive behind-the-scenes look at the meticulous preparation process, from the double marination of the meat to the layering of the rice and the addition of aromatic spices. The highlight of the video is undoubtedly the tasting, where the host eloquently describes the subtle flavors, tender meat, and the perfect balance of spices in both the chicken and mutton biryani.  What sets Niyaaz biryani apart is the subtle character of the biryani, a departure from the typical spice-heavy expectation. This biryani, with its aromatic blend of 52 spices, offers a mellow yet flavorful experience that lingers on the palate long after the meal is over
